subsubtopic: OBSERVANCE OF ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today we join a quarter of the world's people in observing Commonwealth Day. As you know, Mr. Speaker, Canada has been very active in the Commonwealth over the past year. Last October we hosted the heads of Government meeting in Vancouver. Last month the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) chaired the first meeting of the Commonwealth Committee of Foreign Ministers on Southern Africa, created at Vancouver.
Canada continues to be one of the strongest supporters of the Commonwealth. It has given us easy, privileged access to a large group of Third World countries, all of whom were, like Canada, once members of the British Empire. Our Commonwealth experience has provided inspiration for Canada to seek parallel institutions to cement our ties with the Frenchspeaking world. That experience was part of the reason we hosted the Francophone Summit last year in Quebec City.
The Vancouver meeting of the heads of Government of the Commonwealth reviewed the multi-faceted activities of the organization. It addressed major international political and economic issues ranging from Third World debt, to the status of women in society, to the threat to low-lying states from rising water levels.
Canadian Development Assistance, a major dimension of our foreign policy and international identity, has its roots in the Colombo plan of the early 1950s. Today, the Commonwealth Fund for Technical Co-operation, CFTC, provides technical assistance to all parts of the developing Commonwealth.
The fund is virtually unique in that almost all members contribute, and it makes maximum use of experts from developing countries. Canada is the single largest donor to the CFTC, providing approximately $17.5 million in 1987-88, well over one-third of its total resources.
As the meeting in Vancouver demonstrated, the Commonwealth not only consults on major world issues but takes concerted action. The meeting launched three important initiatives.
First, it adopted a new plan of action for southern Africa including assistance to the Front Line States and Mozambique. A committee of eight foreign ministers was established, chaired by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. It was created to provided impetus and guidance in the Commonwealth's struggle against apartheid in South Africa. It has already proved to be a valuable forum in responding to South Africa's recent restrictive actions against opposition groups.
Second, it issued a declaration on world trade to encourage a more liberalized global trading system and reinforce the current round of multilateral trade negotiations. Canada also wrote off the official debt of the poorest Commonwealth African countries.
Third, it endorsed an imaginative scheme for Commonwealth collaboration in distance education based on a Canadian initiative to promote the exchange of information, training, technical assistance and research in the application of distance education techniques at post secondary and vocational levels in the developing Commonwealth countries.
These three initiatives illustrate the breadth of the Commonwealth contribution. The organization we honour today, in which we find common ground and purpose with a billion people in countries large and small around the world, is worthy of our enthusiastic and abiding support.

subsubtopic: OBSERVANCE OF ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Official Opposition takes pleasure in joining with the Hon. Minister of Veterans Affairs and Minister of State for Senior Citizens in his statement celebrating the Commonwealth and its accomplishments in the past and certainly its aspirations for the future. But we would want to take careful note that the Commonwealth at this point in its history faces perhaps its most serious challenge and a serious difficulty. We should not simply celebrate by fond rhetoric or past memories. We should in our rededication apply the principles upon which the Commonwealth has been built and use it as a way of encouraging this Government through its position of leadership in the Commonwealth to continue to press for the kinds of efforts and initiatives to deal with the ever-growing seriousness of the problem in South Africa.

March 14, 1988
Statements by Ministers
Each night we see a further escalation of the conflict of oppression and a denial of all the values to which we adhere. It is for that reason as you know, Mr. Speaker, that our own Party has called clearly for the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) to live up to the commitments he made almost two years ago at the United Nations to take a more forceful and dramatic step in dealing with both economic and diplomatic sanctions.
I noted with some interest that on Saturday night in an address the Prime Minister indicated that the Government is now reviewing its position, something we have called for it to do over the last several weeks. We hope the Government will.
We believe the position that Canada occupies in the Commonwealth is an important one. The steps we take in relation to South Africa will obviously have a major influence and impact upon decisions of other countries in the Commonwealth. We recognize, I think, to be candid, that the leadership of Great Britain at the present time takes a different point of view, but this may be the time for us to demonstrate that the new generation of Commonwealth leadership has a different perspective than that espoused by Mrs. Thatcher. We use this occasion of the statement of the Minister to add our voice of urgency and the sense of need for the Government of Canada through the Commonwealth to demonstrate to the rest of the world that the actions of the South African Government are not to be tolerated and that apartheid must come to an end.
The Minister made reference to both aid and trade as a characteristic of the Commonwealth which should be noted and celebrated. I agree with him again in principle but raise questions about the Government's willingness to follow through on it. I take note that trade with many of the countries in the Commonwealth has fallen drastically over the past three years. Trade with African countries has dropped almost 25 per cent. We have not undertaken the kind of multilateral international trade initiatives that would be required to come to grips with our debt problems in a significant way. More important, we should be creative and imaginative in opening up new trade opportunities with Third World countries, many of which are Commonwealth partners.
I think it is important for this House to note just how drastic has been the shrinkage in trade around the world, other than with the United States. I can only conclude it is because of the particular pre-occupation which the Government has with that trading relationship that the others are being ignored.
I would say as well on the issue of aid that again we applaud the objectives but have questions about the practice. The statement made last week by the Minister for External Relations (Mrs. Landry) setting out new guidelines for the CIDA programs by the Government of Canada has once again set back even further our intention to raise our foreign aid commitment to 0.7 per cent of GNP. The promise made in the 1984 election has now gone through a successive series of further delays and restraints.
In conclusion, the Commonwealth deserves celebration, but it also deserves clear and forthright action in the area of politics, trade and aid. We would encourage the Government to make better use of the Commonwealth than we believe has been made up to this point in time.

subsubtopic: OBSERVANCE OF ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my colleagues in the New Democratic Party, I too would like to join with the Minister of Veterans Affairs, (Mr. Hees), the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) and all Members of the House in observing Commonwealth Day.
New Democrats have a long history of support for global multilateral institutions, including the United Nations and the Commonwealth, because we believe these organizations to be the most effective means at our disposal to address global concerns, whether they be economic, social, military or environmental. However, the Commonwealth is unique.
Born out of conquest and colonialism, the Commonwealth has become a model of international co-operation based on shared values that transcend race, religion and culture. In this respect, the Commonwealth is, perhaps more than any other international institution, an example of how one billion diverse people can put aside their differences and, indeed, the sometimes bitter history they share to work together in the pursuit of common goals.
The Minister has outlined some of the many co-operative endeavours of the Commonwealth, such as the Commonwealth fund for technical co-operation, efforts to liberalize trade, debt restructuring, and the list goes on and on. In many of these areas, Canada has become a Commonwealth leader, some even say that Canada has become the Commonwealth leader. This is a testament to our own commitment as a nation to multicul-turalism, tolerance and social justice.
In some areas, however, the Commonwealth has not been as successful as many would like. A case in point is that of South Africa. While the Commonwealth has been one of the sharpest critics of apartheid in South Africa, concrete efforts on the part of the Commonwealth to bring about change in South Africa have been modest. This, of course, is partly due to the very diversity within the Commonwealth that we generally applaud. However, the system of apartheid in South Africa is so abhorrent to the world community, including the Commonwealth, and the prospect of violence is so great, that I call on the Commonwealth to redouble its efforts to bring about meaningful change in South Africa. In this respect, we believe the Canadian Government must provide even greater leadership, both independently and with other Commonwealth countries.
We believe the Commonwealth has demonstrated that the people of the world can put aside differences and work together for a better global future. We also believe the Commonwealth and the world community as a whole can, and should do more in this regard.
March 14, 1988

We are happy to join with all Canadians in observing Commonwealth Day and we look forward to greater cooperation and concerted global action on the part of the Commonwealth in the future.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have the honour and privilege of presenting a petition signed by residents of Chatham and St. Thomas, Ontario.
The petitioners point out that the Conservative Government had no mandate from the Canadian people to conduct a free trade agreement with the United States and, furthermore, that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised, in the course of the bilateral trade negotiations, that Canadian sovereignty would not be compromised.
In view of the fact that the proposed trade agreement would deny Canada the policy freedom to determine its own economic future and would undermine our ability to build a society distinct from that of the United States, the petitioners therefore call upon Parliament to dissolve and allow the people of Canada the opportunity to accept or reject this proposed trade agreement during a national general election.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 am glad to have the opportunity to add my thoughts and observations to those of my colleagues from other Parties concerning Bill C-82, the Bill proposing the registration of lobbyists in Canada.
This Bill represents the culmination of a legislative movement that has been fermenting and growing within the House of Commons and, indeed, within Canada for some time now. This movement has seen the introduction in the House of several Private Members' Bills dealing with the registration of lobbyists, principally, of course, presented by members of my Party, including one presented by our Party's spokesman for consumer and corporate affairs, the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez).
Finally, the pressure of public opinion in respect of legislative initiative led the Government to realize that this was a matter of serious concern and import to a large number of Canadians. Consequently, in September of 1985, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), in the context of a fairly wide-ranging statement on public-sector ethics, announced the Government's intention to have lobbyists registered. I think it is well worth the time to excerpt some of the statements the Prime Minister made in that open letter.
March 14, 1988

Along with instructions to Ministers on the hiring of family members, the conflict of interest post-employment code for public office holders and the experimental program of parliamentary scrutiny of Governor in Council appointments, on which the jury is still out since we have only had limited experience of it, the Prime Minister included as point five of his open letter the registration of lobbying activity. In expanding on that theme, he stated that we will require, among other things, paid lobbyists to register and identify their clients.
Within the life of the Government there has certainly been bad publicity surrounding the activities of lobbyists. Elowever, let us not forget that in previous Liberal Governments similar activity took place, attracting similar publicity, and justly so, because there were often cases where it was felt that people, for hire or for reward, had undertaken a key role in influencing legislation, its design or structuring programs, their drafting and implementation, and even the timing of regulations in some cases.
My Party is in broad agreement with the legislation the Government has introduced in Bill C-82. We are glad that the time has finally come when Canada will have a regime of registration of lobbyists that will allow Canadians comparable access to the sort of information that our cousins in the U.S. have had for many years; that is, information on who is trying to influence the Government, who is drawing a salary, remuneration or reward for their activities in trying to influence the process of Government, and who is buying the services of these lobbyists. They are known as lobbyists because of the tradition that they operate within the lobbies of this very Chamber. We will know who is paying them and what are their objectives.
First and foremost I think we should say that our Party is quite dubious about the value of the Tier I and Tier II formats that this Bill establishes. We would like to see all lobbyists disgorge the sort of information being demanded from Tier I lobbyists, who we might see as the full-time professional, freelance lobbyists, those who are always up for hire, so to speak, for sale to the highest bidder, compared with the Tier II lobbyists who are largely those instructed by their employers, professional associations, corporate business and trade associations, to seek not only specific legislative initiatives but also to broadly influence the climate of opinion, the focus of debate, the movement and interplay of ideas within Government and Parliament. Some of those lobbyists would have the facility, indeed, in some cases to be more influential than those who move from client to client or who, like many of the leading lobbying firms, have a number of clients on retainer and draw specific fees for specific assignments. Canadians are entitled to know who is doing what, who they are doing it for, who they are talking to, and how much money is changing hands on account of this lobbying.
Lobbying, of course, is a practice which has always been carried on, but in recent years it has become professionalized,
Lobbyists Registration Act
commercialized, and much more organized as well as much more recognized. Some 40 or 50 years ago people might undertake to act for some nominal recognition or compensation by way of intermediary in an age when communications were much less developed. When contact on a direct basis with a Member of Parliament or a member of the Government was certainly much more difficult than it is now, people might undertake to meet the Minister or Member of Parliament or even the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) within the lobby of the House and raise the concern of an individual or the legislative request of a group or body. Now, despite the fact that it is surely easier than it ever has been for the ordinary citizen, company, trade union or association, provincial Government or professional agency to contact members of the Government or organizations within our Parliament, we have this professionalization, and perhaps that is a word I am using a little loosely, but certainly this commercialization of the lobbying process which seems to have no end to it, which seems to be continually growing.
It was alleged back in 1985, and this may have something to do with the introduction of this legislation, that a company which has already been named here accepted a commission of some $2,000 to arrange a meeting between a fisherman and the then Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. This is an example, surely, of the type of lobbying which really should be eliminated, along with a recognition that there are indeed legitimate types of lobbying and very legitimate lobbying objectives.
It seems that most lobbying occurs in secrecy. That is one of the problems this Bill is designed to address. Academic literature indicates that the bureaucracy is the subject of roughly 40 per cent of lobbying activity, and Canadians have to examine whether or not that constitutes an undercutting of the role of Parliament in the policy process. To the extent that Members of Parliament are lobbied, they are often not aware of the role of the individual who makes the contact as a paid lobbyist on a commercial basis. They are often not informed or not aware as to how representative the client group doing the lobbying indeed is.
The American experience is instructive, not simply because of the common language we use or indeed the many similarities between our cultures and our geographic proximity. It is instructive because it is the best documented, the most obvious, and arguably the most widespread example of the lobbying phenomena that the world affords. To quote a former American Senator, Mr. Abraham Ribicoff, in 1975 he said that to protect the democratic process itself, and assure public confidence in it, the lobbyist must work in the open. His work must not be cloaked in secrecy. Secrecy inevitably spreads public suspicion. That has been the objective of the NDP in putting forward Bills on this topic and in addressing this Bill. Lobbying activity should be brought out in the open.
However, I think we must emphasize that a lobby registry is not aimed at policing or restricting access to Government, but merely to make sure those interested in knowing the nature of this access can have access to the information and can know

March 14, 1988
Lobbyists Registration Act
the lines along which paid commercial lobbying within the country is proceeding.
We have had one comprehensive study of lobbying which proposed a model for a lobby registry. I am talking of course of the unanimous report submitted in 1987 by the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure which studied the issue for approximately one year. It visited lobbying registries in various parts of the U.S., including Washington and Sacramento.
We also have to look at indirect lobbying. Members of Parliament, I am sure all of us, will be familiar with the recent case where apparently original letters were distributed very widely by the tobacco companies or their proxies so that these could be signed by individuals and submitted to give the appearance of a mass campaign. The literary style, the use of a limited number of type faces, the structure and phrasing and contextualization of the return addresses, and indeed the addresses these were sent to, soon gave away this mass mailing lobbying campaign. I think we should be looking very hard at the nature of those campaigns and whether they constitute a form of lobbying.
The proposed lobby registry could be given much sharper teeth with which to enforce this legislation. It is conceivable that the fines provided for in the legislation, because of the potential profit in the business, could simply be seen as a form of toll-gating to stay in the game. It is conceivable, after all, that lobbying firms could be organized on a partnership basis, could form and reform in order to get around any strictures put on them. Although, of course, a challenge on the basis of freedom of expression is foreseeable, the Government has to protect the integrity of the governmental and democratic processes, complex as these have become.
Another defect that we see is the lack of power for the Assistant Deputy Registrar General to investigate the information which he or she is given. We believe that the lack of investigatory power would be a handicap and that the ADRG should have the opportunity to review and verify any information that is given.
We have often heard opposition to new legislative initiatives on the grounds of the bureaucracy that would be created by them. I am glad to say that it appears, from the United States experience, that the operation of a lobby registry should not be a major imposition upon the bureaucracy and should not lead to the creation of a large bureaucratic machine. Apparently the American lobby registry in Washington, handling information for over 10,000 lobbyists, is staffed by only three people, which gives us a good idea of what can be done in the computer age.
As I have said previously, this Bill does not provide for prohibition of commercial lobbying, nor should it. However, there is one form of commercial lobbying at which I think we should look very hard to determine whether we want to see it
continued; that is, lobbying on the basis of contingency fee whereby if the lobbyist is successful in obtaining a certain conclusion the fee will be larger than if the lobbyist is unsuccessful, in which case the lobbyist may get no fee.
It is to be noted that within our legal system contingency fees are not permitted on that basis and we think they should be prohibited in the practice of lobbying as well.
We see this piece of legislation providing for the registration of lobbyists as essential, not only in buttressing the integrity of the democratic and governmental process but also in allowing the continuance of the legitimate activities of commercial lobbyists and the legitimate paid activities that they will undertake.
With regard to structuring the lobbying legislation, there is one final thing that I would like to note; that is, once a lobbying registration system is in use it appears that there is very little pressure from the lobbying industry or lobbying community, if you like, to drop the system. It appears that it is something to which the industry is well able to adapt, that given the lighter public scrutiny this is in some cases, and in the cases of the longest established operations, seen as a benefit in that there is no longer a need for the light of suspicion to be cast on them when the information is freely, publicly, and openly available as to who their clients are, what objectives they are seeking, and who they are influencing or seeking to influence within the Government.
In conclusion, Madam Speaker, we see faults and deficiencies within this piece of legislation, but we see it as legislation which Canada needs in order to protect the integrity of the process of government and the operations of democracy in an era when lobbying is becoming far more prevalent, far more pervasive and, we may opine, far more successful.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I too want to avail myself of this opportunity to make some comments on Bill C-82.1 join with my colleague who has just spoken in indicating that we in the Liberal Party as well endorse Bill C-82 in principle. Indeed, it is a giant step in the right direction to begin the lobbying process.
Veteran Members of this House, certainly those with more experience than I, will recall that over the last few decades various private Members in all three Parties have made attempts to see legislation pass this House requiring the registration of lobbyists. Indeed, this Bill is long overdue.
Since I have some concerns about this Bill, and in order that my comments not be misunderstood, let me say that the Liberal Party is prepared to have this Bill passed at this stage of debate in order for it to go to committee. It is our hope that in committee some improvements can be made to Bill C-82 by all-Party consensus. It is my understanding, although I was not a member of the Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure which worked on this, that indeed all three Parties worked well to produce the recommendations out of which flowed the legislation that is now before us.
March 14, 1988

We do have some problems with the Bill. As has been said by earlier speakers, the Bill sets up two categories of lobbyists. Basically I do not have much problem with one of the categories. I am not one of those who believes that every single person who wants to make representations to government on behalf of a particular employee group or association which they represent must, in massive detail, provide information to a registry in Ottawa. However, with regard to the registration of lobbyists of the kind which are best personified by the Frank Moores operation in Ottawa, which have evolved over the last couple of years, and indeed there are others, I think this Bill does not go far enough.
Let me begin by talking about the registration process for lobbyists contained in this Bill. Most Canadians who are watching this debate are saying that it is a good thing to make lobbyists register, that the people who traditionally operate in the shadowed, smokey back rooms will now have to come out into the full glaring light of day and register. They are saying that that is a good thing.
Canadians should know that there is no provision in the Bill that lobbyists register who they are making contact with and on whose behalf. There is no provision in the Bill to give the designated registrar the authority to check the information that is being registered. In other words, it is an act of faith. Information is provided and there is no mechanism or authority in this Bill to check the information which is being registered.
There is a larger problem. The Bill recommends that the Assistant Deputy Registrar General be the authority empowered to hold this information, be the registrar for lobbyists. That is a very impressive sounding title and Canadians should be asking who is the Assistant Deputy Registrar General. Is it someone like the Auditor General, an independent officer of Parliament who is not directly under the direction or authority of the Government or the Opposition? Is that who the Assistant Deputy Registrar General is? No, that is not who he is. He is not like the Auditor General.
The Assistant Deputy Registrar General is a civil servant. He is an employee of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. His job, indeed his career path, is not independent of the Government, his Minister, or political consideration. His job, his career path, is directly linked, or at least can be directly linked to the happiness or unhappiness of his political masters.
Why am I raising this point about who this authority is going to be?
Canadians will recall that a few months ago the present Assistant Deputy Registrar General stated that certain Conservative Party moneys made available to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) were subject to the conflict of interest guidelines and should have been registered. This statement was made on Friday and headlines throughout
Lobbyists Registration Act
Canada were that a Minister of the Crown, in this case the Prime Minister, had not complied with the conflict of interest guidelines. By Monday the Prime Minister produced in the House of Commons a letter by the same Assistant Deputy Registrar General saying that there had been no violation of the conflict of interest guidelines. That rather dramatic conversion did not really upset Members of the House. In fairness to the gentleman involved, perhaps upon reflection he had come to the conclusion that his statements on Friday were ill conceived and, therefore, clarified the matter on Monday.
However, what did upset Parliament and every right thinking Canadian was that, despite repeated requests for a clarification, a briefing or explanation for the ruling of the Assistant Deputy Registrar General on Monday, he refused to give one. When we asked to which clause and which section of the conflict of guidelines we should refer to understand the dramatically different ruling he gave from the one three days earlier, we were met with silence. In the interest of fairness, I personally called this gentleman on the telephone but was merely told that he could not comment.
I was not going to speak on this Bill until I read in the Bill that the authority in whom shall be vested all of the information required under Bill C-82 is the same Assistant Deputy Registrar General. I have a serious problem with the Bill in those circumstances.
I do not question the integrity or the honesty of the gentleman who holds the job. In fairness to him, I suggest that he is in a difficult position because he does not have the protection of an independent, arm's length relationship with the Government like that held by the Auditor General, an ability to be accountable only to Parliament as a whole rather than to any particular political party.
The gentleman who must hold this job is a public servant. According to this Bill, a civil servant is being asked to assume a quasi judicial authority and to exercise a measure of independence. Yet this is made impossible by the fact that he is indeed a public servant who is dependent upon the goodwill of his Minister and the Government that he serves.
Therefore, my first point is that the authority in whom shall reside the information and the responsibility to police this legislation cannot be a public servant, no matter how flamboyant his title. The authority in whom the information required under the lobbying Bill shall reside must be an officer of Parliament who is independent of any consideration to the Government, the Opposition, whether Conservative, New Democratic or Liberal. Only then can Parliament and, more important, the people of Canada be assured that the registration of the information provided and the enforcement of the rules will be above board. I believe this is a matter that Members of the House will want to address and improve when this Bill goes to committee.
There are a number of other fundamental flaws in the Bill that I believe Members of all Parties will want to address,

March 14, 1988
Lobbyists Registration Act
because I believe there is goodwill among Members of every Party to pass legislation that works well.
There is no provision in the Bill to deal with the question of fees of lobbyists for activities they conduct on behalf of a client. Canadians should be aware of an interesting new wrinkle that has evolved in the last few years with respect to the activities of lobbyists. One originally thought of lobbyists as people who would accept a fee to go to a Minister of the Crown of the government of the day and make one's case as best they could, to make one's views known about a piece of legislation, to request new legislation or amendments to current legislation in an attempt to influence the decision a government might make in a matter of national or public importance. This is quite acceptable, providing those lobbyists are registered.
However, the new practice, which is best personified by the work of the Frank Moores' operation in Ottawa, involves contingency fees. For example, Mr. Moores may tell a client that he will take on a case for $1,000 but, if successful, will then be paid another $10,000. This practice means that not only is there a payment for supposedly professional services to make the case in a lobbying effort, there is an additional payment if that effort is successful. I believe that most Canadians are not aware of this practice and simply think of contingency fees as another Ottawa buzz word. Contingency fees means that one pays the lobbyists for making the case and pays much more if the lobbyist wins the case.
Surely a contingency fee system in which a lobbyist may be paid tenfold his initial fee for successfully making the case on behalf of an individual or corporation is a temptation to be less than forthright in those lobbying efforts. Suddenly, the lobbyist no longer uses all his professional skills for a certain fee. Lobbyists now face the prospect of making substantially more money if their lobbying is successful. I submit that such a system in which substantial amounts can be made-perhaps $500,000 or even $5 million-creates an atmosphere and the potential for corruption, and the exchange of rewards or gifts becomes much more likely. It is not now simply someone doing his best to make a case, but someone who knows that the financial reward is fantastic if he is successful and the temptation to do whatever is necessary to get the right decision will rise dramatically. The whole matter of contingency fees which is being practised, as I say, foremost by the Frank Moores firm, but perhaps by others, is not dealt with in this Bill.
There is another matter of great concern with respect to Bill C-82, at which I think Members, particularly those who made the recommendations out of which flowed Bill C-82, will want to have a very serious look. In essence, the Bill sets up a system in which the only person required to register as a lobbyist is the individual who, for a fee or, in the case I just mentioned, a contingency fee-and that should be made illegal-makes a representation to the Government. That is a lobbyist, someone
who is making a case. That allows a broad group of people to escape having to register as having had a lobbyist in Ottawa. Unless the lobbyist is actually making a case on behalf of a client he is not required to register.
What is the problem, you ask, Madam Speaker? What about the firm which hires a lobbyist not to make a case to the federal Government on its behalf but to merely solicit information? They are not asking for anything to be changed or for a piece of legislation, nor are they asking for an amendment to a decision. They only want information. For example, a real estate speculator hires a lobbyist, giving him a yearly fee. He does not want any lobbying done. That lobbyist, who is now not required to register because he is not making a case for anyone, in the course of his business discovers that an airport is to be built at a particular site or that a new highway is going to be re-routed in a certain way. He gives that information to the real estate firm which promptly goes out and buys all the land in the vicinity, realizing a huge profit on that insider information.
Under the provisions of this Bill, because no representation was made, that lobby effort is not required to be registered. Parliament has no right to know that a particular individual, who made a profit because of access to insider information, was being represented or had a lobbyist acting on his behalf in the nation's capital. The Bill is specifically worded to say that a lobbyist must only report when he is acting in a representative capacity. There is nothing about an advisory capacity. There is nothing in the Bill with respect to a lobbyist who provides insider information, all of which flows from the individuals, groups, departments and directors of Parliament Hill. He is exempt.
I submit to you, Madam Speaker, and to Members, that that kind of lobbying, the indirect kind of lobbying, the exchange of information kind of lobbying, is perhaps more potentially susceptible to illegal practices and fantastic profits because of privileged information than is direct lobbying where it is up front. That is another area which I believe the committee has to consider and make amendments.
I said at the beginning that my Party and I support this Bill. We support it because a baby must learn to walk before it can run. This Bill takes us into the process so that we can begin to walk. Certainly, if it is to be a good Bill, there is room, and I hope there is the will, to substantially amend it at committee stage.

Yes, Madam Speaker, there are a number of other changes I would like to see made to the Bill. First, the Bill does not require, as currently drafted, that there be a record of official contacts. No record whatsoever is required to be kept in the event at a later date of some questioning or some
March 14, 1988

unusual circumstances arising with respect to a particular Government transaction. We are not going to be able to go back in the records to see who was acting for whom and what contacts were made because that is not required in the Bill.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak on this important Bill for western Canada. I am also appreciative of the fact that this debate today is somewhat unconventional. I think it is important, though, that all sides of the House do agree that we have the opportunity to debate more fully a law which is so important for western Canada.
Our Party is in support of the principle of the Bill. We have long been calling for diversification of the western economy. We are in support of the principle of decentralization of the powers for doing this in western Canada. However, we question the Government's commitment. How seriously is the Government taking the whole question of western diversification? I will be looking more closely at the fact that only $1.2 billion is estimated to be spent on this initiative in the next five years.
From the time of Confederation there have been policies in Canada to encourage regional development. They have been an important part of Canadian politics. Even the Constitution Act of 1867 called for the building of the Intercolonial Railway, which was an important regional development initiative at that time.
John A. Macdonald's national policy, when it was fully developed, had not only the element of a tariff structure to encourage industry formation in central Canada, but it also called for the building of the CPR as a link to the Pacific and the developing of the Pacific coast. As well there was the Dominion Lands Act which looked to the opening up of the Prairies. We had the development of the Crow's Nest rate to help agriculture on the Prairies.
In spite of these initiatives that have been taken from time to time in the last 20 years we have become very much aware of continuing disparities. Eastern Canada suffers from lower wages and from higher rates of unemployment than other parts of Canada. Western Canada has had a boom and bust economy. Indeed, many Members might recall the famous analogy that Tommy Douglas used about Canada being like a cow. He said it was fed in the West, milked in central Canada and God only knows what it is doing in the Maritimes, in eastern Canada.
Patricia Marchak, a UBC economist, has pointed to some of the problems in the economy of British Columbia. She points to our great dependence upon the forest industry. She says that

March 14, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
the relative positions of primary metals, metal fabricating, chemicals, printing and publishing, foods, non-metallic minerals and electric products have declined in the last few years. The positions of transportation equipment, non-electric machinery and, of course, petroleum products have improved. Others have remained constant.
She states:
Considering the enormous wealth created in British Columbia during this decade, the expansion of timberlands under production, and the amount of forestry products exported the growth in secondary industries is not impressive.
She also stated:
Signally missing from the regional landscape are firms manufacturing pulpmill machinery, chemicals, and computer equipment: all high-value, technologically advanced equipment and supplies for the pulping sector... Pulpmill machinery and computer equipment, however, are important... Total employment in secondary manufacturing was estimated by Statistics Canada to be 77,000-6 per cent of the labour force.
Relative to the total labour force, workers in metal fabricating and transportation equipment combined were 1 per cent. Chemicals, machinery-industries, electrical products, and non-metallic mineral products-the other sectors that might be expected to generate new employment in a forestry-dependent region-were negligible as employers-
The same is true of consumer products unrelated to forestry. Apart from food and beverages, B.C. does not have a substantial consumer products industry. There are small companies producing textiles, clothing, furniture and fixtures, leather goods, and other, more miscellaneous goods but the vast majority of household goods and personal consumer items purchased are manufactured elsewhere.
Professor Marchak points to the dangers of depending upon a staples economy. She states that the so-called theories of comparative advantage might work to the interests of the companies that are developing the resource and exploiting the resource. If there is an international downturn, then they can take their profits and move them elsewhere. This type of dependence upon single industries, this dependence upon basic resources, has not served the people of western Canada well.
Perhaps this is as good a way as any for us to understand the continuing and growing bitter debate in British Columbia between those people who are concerned about resource extraction and those who are concerned about questions such as environmental protection or land claims. What we have in British Columbia is a great deal of pressure upon a resource base that has been exploited over the last number of years without too much thought for the future. We are now getting back to logging and mining in areas that should never have been logged or mined. These are areas that are ecologically sensitive. They are areas that are sacred and of symbolic as well as economic importance to the aboriginal peoples of British Columbia.
Because we have not taken advantage of the wealth that has been created over the past 100 years by the exploitation of the forest industry and the mining industry, which has been largely hived off to other areas, and because we have not diversified, we as a province continue to be highly dependent upon those extractive resources. We are now moving into areas in which there are great social conflicts. Thus it is important
that we have regional development policies that address this type of boom and bust economy in western Canada.
The problems of regional development in western Canada are different from those in Atlantic Canada. The Government recognizes this when it talks about a western economic diversification fund. What we need is economic diversification. Over the past number of years different Governments have tried different approaches to the whole business of economic diversification. In a study that was prepared for the Macdonald Commission by Norie, Simeon and Krasnick, entitled Federalism and the Economic Union of Canada, the authors have summarized the different approaches. They speak of three continuing tensions in the area of the economic development.
First, Canadians have never been able to come up with theories or policies, or even projects, that appeared to work. Policy has staggered from being oriented toward sectors, as in ARDA, to being oriented to area economic development more generally, including adjustment out of the region-that is helping people to move away from depressed areas-to orientation toward growth poles, ADA and DREE. Programs have ranged from adjustment assistance to infrastructure grants, to tax breaks, to direct subsidies, to regionally differentiated investment and employment credits.
Second, we have never settled on the proper relation between federal and provincial responsibilities for regional economic development. Early federal efforts were highly centralized and tended to ignore provincial wishes. During the GDA period almost the reverse was true. The federal Government paid the tab for province building. The pendulum again swung in the opposite direction for a brief period, and today it remains in motion.
Finally, the federal Government has never managed to link its regional development responsibilities satisfactorily with its broader national economic management role. The best manifestation of its failure is the constant rearranging of the federal bureaucracy, first to bring regional interests into a separate department, then to make all departments consider regional implications implicitly, and finally to drift back to the single ministry concept.
So what we have had over the last number of years is a constant shifting from one kind of program to another. Sometimes the shifts have been more apparent than real. Sometimes they have been real shifts. We have moved back and forth between talking about regions to talking about provinces and so on. It remains to be seen whether the initiative that we have in Bill C-113 to establish the western diversification fund will come to grips with these problems representing a long term, sustained commitment to deal with the problems of the needs of the western economy for diversification.
March 14, 1988

The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has said that previous efforts at regional development have not worked and that we cannot simply solve the problem by throwing money at it. However, the federal-provincial task force on regional development assessment, prepared for the First Ministers' Economic Conference last November, pointed out that the resources supplied to regional development over the past 25 years have been small in relative terms. We have not thrown that much money at the problem.
Expenditures for Canada were in the order of 3 per cent of total federal economic expenditures and are now less than that. Greater expenditures could well have had significantly greater results. Regional development efforts in the 1970s were successful in the context of the amount of resources applied to them. In other words, we got what we paid for. Under the new diversification fund we will get what we pay for. If we do not put much money in, we will not get very much out of it.
It has also been shown that the actions of federal line Departments can have a very much greater impact than specific regional development programs because of their greater expenditure base. The frequently expressed negative view of regional development programs is due, to a great extent, to the expectations raised by such programs. Results must be judged on the resources used to achieve them rather than on total needs.
We are concerned that there is a great deal of hype about western diversification and the fact that the Government is decentralizing and establishing an office in Edmonton, as well as regional offices in Vancouver, Saskatoon, and Winnipeg. There is a build-up of expectation. However, when we look for a commitment of funds, we find that the commitment is not there. The sum of $1.2 billion over five years amounts to some $60 million per year for each of the four western provinces. It is not really very much money.
In 1977 the Economic Council of Canada pointed out that even the highly controversial program of incentive grants to influence companies to locate in the Atlantic area had had modest success. Again I say that we get some return for the money we are prepared to spend, but we cannot make a silk purse out of a sow's ear. If the Government is not prepared to spend money in this area, it cannot expect that there will be significant successes in terms of development.
Since the 1981-82 recession we have seen dramatic growth in the economy of central Canada, particularly that of southern Ontario. The regions of Canada have been much slower in recovering. Indeed, in parts of Canada it would be a mistake to speak of recovery at all. In my area on Vancouver Island the number of unemployed, according to the latest jobless figures, is exactly the same as it was in September, 1984, so we cannot speak of a recovery.
When we look at Bill C-l 13 we are concerned about the lack of a clear government strategy in terms of what it is really
Western Economic Diversification Act
encouraging the western economy to do. It talks about flexibility. Certainly our Party supports the concept of flexibility in the way in which the diversification fund should be applied. As admirable as flexibility is as a goal and a means, it should not be used as justification for lack of a clear policy. We do not see that clear policy in what the Government has announced.
Over the last 3.5 years we have seen an increase in the percentage of DRIE funds going to central Canada and we have seen 47 per cent of all jobs created going to Ontario. The Government seems to be letting the economy drift and is now making a modest effort at diversification, but we do not see the required commitment.
Last summer the New Democratic Party, led by the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) and the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), released its own paper on economic diversification for the West. I should like to refer to some of the points that we made.
First, we should be adding value to western resources. There are many opportunities for creating new industries and new jobs in upgrading or adding value to our natural resource exports. Of course, a good example of that would be the lumber industry, as well as the petrochemical and food processing sectors.
Second, we should do more to serve the needs of the resource industry. Earlier I referred to Patricia Marchak who pointed out how complex machinery used in our pulp mills, as well as a great deal of machinery used in our mining and logging industries, is not produced in western Canada but comes from abroad. The West is a major user of machinery and equipment, but we do not produce it ourselves. If we developed industries to serve the resource industries in our part of the country, if we developed the kinds of industries which produced pulp mill, logging, and mining equipment, we could hope that in time these industries would not only be serving local markets but would be expanding and developing into important export industries in their own right.
We also need support for the manufacturing industry in the West. The Government promised to increase procurement in the West. Quite frankly it has a shameful record in that regard. If we look at 1981-82, we see that 15.5 per cent of government procurements came from the four western provinces. In 1982-83, that declined to 14.7 per cent. In 198384, it was a disaster as far as the West was concerned; only 9.8 per cent of procurements were in western Canada. They increased to 13.9 per cent in 1984-85, declined in 1985-86 to 12.8 per cent, and declined again in 1986-87 to 11.5 per cent.
The Government says that it will do something about it, but it has not set any targets or goals. If it were really serious about it, it would be prepared to show its commitment by setting out some kind of affirmative action program for procurement in western Canada. It could set targets and say that it would work toward reaching the proper percentage of purchases in western Canada in proportion to the population

March 14, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
by a certain time. Instead, there is a vague commitment toward procurement policies despite the sorry record of the Government over the last 3.5 years.
It also talked about creating new industries and jobs. Our study pointed out that some of the historic disadvantages of the West, such as long distances from markets and so on, are disappearing because of the development of new industries and high technology. Here is something important in my own area, an area with great natural scenery and a very attractive climate. We should be building upon that kind of resource in attracting new non-polluting industries.
When we look at the expenses in British Columbia, we have to question whether or not the Government is taking seriously new initiatives, or if it is simply using the $1.2 billion to plug loopholes that should have been met from other departmental expenses.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Member. I would like to follow up his last suggestion of environmentally sensitive and good industries. Surely that is the way of the future. He and I are both from British Columbia and we share a real sensitivity to the environment because it is so good. I am sure all Hon. Members will not like it but I can't resist telling everyone that the tulips are out in my backyard in Vancouver. I have an old convertible and the top is down already. Could the Member follow up about money being spent and how it was spent from departmental funds. Also, could he comment on the kind of future industries that he would like to see in British Columbia.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first, the kind of industries we would like to see in the future include the high tech sector. The kind of future industries I am looking for for Vancouver Island are those which take advantage of rapid transportation by air that will not be expensive in weight and volume. On that basis, one of our fundamental economic needs is to preserve the environment of Vancouver Island as a good place for people to live and, therefore, as a good place for industries to locate.
With regard to the money that has already been spent, let us look at three expenses the Government took out of the $1.2 billion last year before the fund got fully operational. First was $79 million over five years for South Moresby Park. Members on all sides of the House supported the creation of South Moresby Park. But should that money necessarily have come out of the Western Diversification Fund?
Second, there was $9.5 million for shakes and shingles market development. The shakes and shingles economy of British Columbia was hit by the 35 per cent tariff imposed by our friends in the United States. In co-operation with the shakes and shingles manufacturers, the Western Diversification Fund is putting $9.5 million trying to expand that market again and perhaps find other markets.
What about the $53 million for the salmon enhancement project? It is this program that I want to question because that $53 million will be spent over the next five years. It will be added to $154.3 million spread over five years, money that will come from the Department of Fisheries and Oceans.
As you know, Madam Speaker, the Salmonoid Enhancement Program has been the responsibility of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. During this last year the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) went to the Cabinet Committee on Economic and Regional Development to tap into the policy reserve funds to the tune of some $50 million per year for the next five years. He was not given that money from the policy reserve fund from where it should have come. Instead, money was made available from the Western Diversification Fund. It is less money than the Minister was seeking, and it is just enough to barely maintain the current project levels. It is important funding.
The Salmonoid Enhancement Program is important to British Columbia. But is there some kind of a hoax being perpetrated on us? This money should have come from the regular Estimates of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans or from policy reserve funds. Instead, the Government makes a great show of announcing extra funding. It is called new money from the Western Diversification Fund but it is going back into what should have come from a line department. This use of the Western Diversification Fund to meet commitments that should be made from other departments, is, I think, a hoax.
While we support the concept and the principle of this Bill, we have to ask whether or not the Government is really committed. It seems the Government is not prepared to put its money where its mouth is in this whole area.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a comment and a question for the Hon. Member. The so-called free trade agreement with the United States has also to be considered in western diversification and regional growth. There is a body of opinion in British Columbia reflected this weekend in the polls shown in The Vancouver Sun. People do not really understand the free trade agreement, although they think it will go through. Although there tends to be a split, the majority are in favour of it. Interestingly enough, a huge majority feel the Americans will benefit by the deal.
I am concerned that a lot of British Columbians do not understand that we never won what British Columbians hoped we would win in the free trade agreement, namely, secure access to the American market. An economy like British Columbia's is an undiversified economy, really, an export economy of raw materials. We will be giving away control of our energy resources and threatening our sovereignty by it, but we are going to take this leap of faith. We should at least have been given a guarantee of access to the American market for our fish and forest products, mining and so on. I do not think we got that in the deal. In fact, I know we do not have it in the
March 14, 1988

deal because I have read it. Congress can still pass countervailing laws that will do the same thing again as was done to our lumber and shakes and shingles industry. Does the Elon. Member have any comment whether the two are intertwined as I think they are?

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, very briefly, I agree 100 per cent with the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell). Not only that, but the western diversification initiative itself along with the regional development program for Atlantic Canada and northern Ontario can be made the subject of controversy over the next five to seven years under this agreement. Canada and the United States have to sit down, bargain and horse trade as to what constitutes an acceptable or unacceptable subsidy. Although from the point of view of western Canada this $1.2 billion is insufficient to help us diversify, in the eyes of the Americans it might seem to be a great deal of money for them to look at as an unjustified subsidy and, therefore, subject to countervail. The Hon. Member is quite right, that we do not have the kind of secure access under the trade agreement that was promised to us by the Prime Minister.

Madam Speaker, when the Bill was called this morning again, as you explained it, I was doing some research on the western Canadian economy. I cannot pass up this opportunity to make some comments about a matter so important for the 7.3 million people who live in the West today. First, I would like to comment about the point my friend from Vancouver- Kingsway made on the trade agreement with which I will deal at some length in a moment.
In view of the fact that there is now an election campaign in Manitoba, I wonder if any of my friends from the New Democratic Party know that Manitoba has a payroll tax under the present New Democratic Government. To my knowledge, Manitoba is the only province in Canada which has such a tax. It is the only-

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext:
The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) has made a comment on behalf of the Liberal Party. It has been so long since there has been a Liberal Party in Manitoba that even my family used to belong to it.
The labour force information that came out this morning gives us figures for the various parts of the country. We see, for example, that Oshawa's unemployment rate is 4.4 per cent. Taking a quick look, I see that that is the lowest figure for any city in Canada. Why is that? Is it because of the Auto Pact, the Auto Pact that will be enshrined in the trade agreement? If the United States wanted to cancel the Auto Pact, which it could do with a year's notice, it would have to cancel the entire trade agreement. That is a point that Liberals and New Democrats might contemplate.
In the West, the unemployment rate in Winnipeg is 8.5 per cent in Regina it is 6.2 per cent, in Saskatoon it is 12.6 per cent, in Calgary it is 8.0 per cent, in Edmonton it is 11.6 per cent, in Vancouver it is 9.7 per cent and in Victoria it is 11.9 per cent. Let us compare that with Toronto which has an unemployment rate of 3.9 per cent.
We cannot have a united country when the unemployment rate is higher in Newfoundland, New Brunswick and western Canada than it is elsewhere. That is why all of us in western Canada want to do something about creating more opportunities for young and for middle-aged people. That is the way to build a country with strong, diversified economies in the Maritimes and western Canada.
The old national policy of Sir John A. Macdonald and Wilfrid Laurier created strong, diversified, stable economies in central Canada. Those of us in outer Canada now feel it is time we had a new national policy which would do the same things for the other eight provinces and the North. I believe that this Bill is a step in the direction a new national policy would be required to take.
It was asked whether or not the trade agreement will help the West. Hon. Members will notice that three of the four western premiers are strongly in favour of the proposed trade agreement. I trust that on April 26, four premiers from western Canada will be in favour of it.
Business groups, farming groups and western Canadians everywhere believe that this is our chance to have an opportunity, not just for western Canadians but for all Canadians, to have more stability, security and discipline in our trading relationships. I wonder if Hon. Members know that between two million and three million Canadians depend upon access to the U.S. market for their livelihoods. Based on the fact that about one-third of the population is in the West, by my arithmetic, about 600,000 western Canadians are dependent upon the U.S. market for their pay cheques. In that sense, whether one is a pensioner, an artist or a provincial public employee, the trade agreement and the promise it offers for the creation and security of employment is very important to all westerners and to all Canadians, in my submission.

March 14, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
Western Canada's major exports to the United States include a good share of the almost $3 billion in agricultural products of all sorts sold by Canadian farmers in the U.S. last year. Our grains, beef, pork, natural gas, oil and potash all have faced barriers. The trade agreement will give us more secure access than we would have otherwise.
Do Hon. Members of the Liberal and New Democratic Parties really think that tearing up the agreement, something which both of them have promised to do, will do anything for their constituents or for western Canada? As someone said the other day, as soon as one of them were to tear up the trade agreement, the new American administration, whether under President Bush or President Dukakis, would simply say, "I have something to tear up for you," and that would be the Auto Pact. I think the support for the trade agreement is strong in western Canada among all thoughtful men and women who want to improve the standard of living in our regions.
It seems to me that the models we should be looking at for western Canada might well be Switzerland, West Germany and Japan. Each of those countries has achieved a high general standard of living and relatively full employment throughout their respective countries by producing a range of high-quality finished products which are exported with major marketing skill and with first-class service to customers. All three populations know that success today in the increasingly interdependent world economy depends on intelligence, quality control and technology, and they act accordingly. I feel that this Bill will move us in this direction, and therefore I think it is one which all Hon. Members should support.
In the West, economic life has historically depended upon things like fish, fur, wheat, beef, forest products, coal, oil, gas and minerals. All of these resource products continue to play a substantial role in our economy. The prosperity of architects, teachers and public employees all depend in a very real way on how these resource products are doing.
Let me give Hon. Members an example of the way one northwestern Canadian put it. Not too long ago he said of a typical Yukon mining development, that the ore goes to Tokyo, the profits to Toronto, the taxes to Ottawa, the jobs to Vancouver, and they are left with a hole in the ground which, if the federal Government gives permission, they could use as a garbage dump. When coal moves to Japan, it comes back as Toyotas or other Japanese cars. Unemployment in that country is virtually non-existent whereas unemployment in the West, as I have indicated before and as we all know, is far too high.
Hon. Members will know that the current prospects for some of the resource sectors such as grains and oilseeds are not as promising as we would like them to be. Therefore, we must come up with a new strategy that will help us create jobs in other sectors.
As an example of what I hope the western diversification strategy will do, I would point to the case of an alfalfa heater
which is being built in my own constituency. I understand that it has a market in Nebraska and someone will pay about half a million dollars for that unit. Someone else in south Edmonton is trying to develop a super computer.
As Members know, we have an extremely talented, highly educated population throughout the west. We have a multicultural population, people from all over the world. Many of them are very entrepreneurial, and many know about other cultures and economies and how we can find a niche in those economies. We have an entrepreneurial dynamism in the west. We have, if you like, a necessity to compete and do well as part of Canada. The ingredients for high technology are all there, as a study by the OECD pointed out. We have a great many things going for us as a region. We have the people, the resources, the will, and this Bill will perhaps give us a little bit more help to put these things in place.
I might say just a few words about oil sands, which are so important to Alberta. If Alberta and western Canada can become the leading centre of oil sands technology in the world we could help develop and build plants in our own region, environmentally sound plants, and go on to help develop oil sands in other parts of the world. We are already using our oil and gas technology in China and the Soviet Union. There is no reason that we cannot build a technology-based superstructure, if you like, in western Canada that would export services around the world.
That is probably where the best hope for the western economy lies. Not to abandon or put aside or stop stressing our resources, but to build a technological base on top of those resources. For example, let me give some suggestions with respect to forestry, since the Hon. Member spoke of it. Why not give further encouragement to harvesting energy from forest biomass? This could be an economic boost for our forest industry and help Canada become a world leader in biomass energy technology. Why not upgrade the importance of the federal Minister responsible for forestry, in part by having him or her responsible for forestry alone? Why not do more research, as I hope we will under this Bill, on things like forest farming on marginal agricultural land and more research into methods of utilizing species such as birch, green ash, willow, alder and soft maples? Why not give some additional federal support to the two forestry schools in western Canada at the University of Alberta and the University of British Columbia? Can we not recruit to public and private forestry service more scientists, more policy analysts and economists? How about more federal funding for western forest renewal through agreements with all four western provinces?
Tourism has been talked about at great length in this House. We could say that British Columbia depends upon three sectors: tourism, forestry and mining. If you reduce U.S. access to all three of those sectors, then you will have calamity in that province. The same for Alberta. Our tourism offers enormous potential. There is potential in Saskatchewan and
March 14, 1988

Manitoba which should be developed. This, as many people have said, is the perfect industry because it brings people in, uses existing facilities, and they leave without pollution. I very much hope that tourism is one area that the western diversification office will look at very carefully because I am told by the end of the century it will be the largest industry in Canada. It offers enormous promise to western Canada.
I must not sit down without saying a word about natural gas. As we know, the industry has had some difficulties. The private sector is understandably reluctant to undertake some of these large oil sands and gas projects because they lack a sense of what the price will be. My suggestion would be that if the difference between the price for some of these oil sands and other projects and the world price could be negotiated in advance, perhaps with the help of the department, it might make the chances of these projects going ahead much better. Security of future supply is so critical that in my view the risk is warranted.
We must give encouragement to new oil sands technology, new ways of separating the sand from the oil. Let me end my remarks with this example because it makes the point probably more strongly than anything I can say and I believe all of this is true. There is an Albertan by the name of Shannon who spent 12 years trying to develop a process for putting coal and bitumen together to produce a clean fuel. I gather within the last several months the method has been perfected. He received I think a $45 million grant from the U.S. Department of Energy to build a plant, not in Canada but in Ohio. It is going to be almost a quarter of a billion dollar plant and it will take Ohio coal and bitumen, and would you believe 85 per cent of it will come from Cold Lake, Alberta by pipeline, put those two together and produce a new clean fuel.
The question that all of us in western Canada ask is, why on earth is that project being built in Ohio? Why is it not being built in Alberta where we have an abundance of both coal and bitumen?
This is the kind of thing I hope this Bill will ensure that we stop doing to ourselves. I hope from this Bill will come an era in which it will be unheard of that anyone would put the first pilot project for a plant to use bitumen and coal somewhere other than western Canada. Therefore, I say in support of the Bill that it is a step in the right direction.
