subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to address once again the issue of western development. I have read with interest the comments of the Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour) who just spoke. I want to compliment him in particular for an article he wrote recently entitled "Policy Options". It was a very thoughtful piece. I did not agree entirely with the content, but I did admire his efforts to put western development into a

March 14, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
framework of analysis, even though I think he fell substantially short on some of his prescriptions.
The Member mentioned how the trade agreement will affect western Canada. It has been heralded by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) as the great salvation for the West. It has been held out as the generator of massive economic growth, all kinds of new initiatives, and development of industry.
Even as late as this weekend the Economic Conference Board has estimated that any expectations for a grand economic bonanza are fallacious. The Department of Finance, now confirmed by the Economic Conference Board, pointed out that the best we can assume, the most optimistic scenario of economic benefits of the trade agreement, is half of 1 per cent of gross per year which, any economitrician will tell you, is within the margin of error of any forecasting model. It is so marginal, so meaningless, as to not even be within the capacity to make an accurate forecast.
This consistent effort to try to paint the trade agreement as being the key which will open economic riches is in fact contradicted, first by the Government's own report put forward by the Department of Finance, and now confirmed by the Economic Conference Board, which in itself supports a trade agreement for other reasons but confirms that any expectation that it will result in huge economic growth is not to be believed.
I suggest that the Hon. Member go back and look at the hard facts, rather than the theology, as presented in his Government's own analysis and in the recent analysis by the Economic Conference Board. It is simply not there. The expectations which were raised over two years ago are not being borne out.
In fact, as the Conference Board itself points out, the Government will be facing a major deficit that will have to be made up by increased taxation. The Conference Board estimates an annual deficit of close to $4 billion cumulative that will have to be made up by increased taxes, or increasing the deficit of the Government itself. It would be very prudent for Conservative Members of Parliament, before talking about the trade agreement, to check their facts. They need not believe me, they need only believe their own Government, their own Department of Finance, and the Economic Conference Board which is a business based group. Those are the prescriptions of those organizations.
Second, it is important to put some perspective as well on whether in fact the free trade agreement will have a specific incentive for regional development. I am often amused by the efforts of the Member for Edmonton-Strathcona and other Conservative Members to make a comparison between the Auto Pact and western Canada. They constantly use the argument that if the Auto Pact was good for Oshawa the free trade agreement should be good for western Canada, as if they were the same thing when in fact they are not. They are quite different, quite contrary trade agreements.
The Auto Pact is a managed trade agreement which carries within it very clear safeguards ensuring that job investment takes place in Canada, whereas the proposed agreement with the Americans contains none of those safeguards. In fact, they have taken the safeguards away from the Auto Pact itself and have put no safeguards in for any other industry. They will be applying the principle of national treatment, which is that there can be no safeguards, preferences, or advantages for Canadian businesses over American businesses. Therefore, any effort to try to make the comparison is fallacious, it does not hold true.
I would only ask the Member, who I believe has a commitment to doing proper research, to look at what happened to various regions in Europe after the Common Market. Has it helped the north of England for example? In fact, the north of England has become more depressed since joining the Common Market than it was before. Certain regions of the southeast portion of France have become more depressed. The Mediere region, for example, has suffered more as a result of that than it did previously. One of the reasons for that is that once you apply a simple market-based system and eliminate the opportunity to undertake public action to provide for a redress of imbalances, of course the forces of the market-place and geography take over and you eliminate the opportunity to have a political economy, to make certain choices from the public sector to compensate for or reallocate the market-place.
That, after all, has been the history of Canada. There would not be a Canada if those choices had not been made. The founders of Confederation from Lower and Upper Canada and the Maritimes formed this country based upon a political choice. They could have easily followed the north-south lines of the market-place and geography but they did not. They wanted to create a different country. Since then we have had to take decisions like building a railroad with great government subsidy from east to west to hold the country together, a public sector communications system, a national health system, and regional development programs. The impact of the trade agreement will be to reduce substantially and limit the capacity of federal and provincial governments to undertake those initiatives.
Let me give the Member for Edmonton-Strathcona an example. He concluded his remarks by talking about a project to turn coal into a new form of energy. There is another coal project which is very important to western Canada, that is, the movement of western Canadian coal to Ontario to be burned in the hydro plants of Ontario in order for them to meet their environmental restraints.
A task force of federal-provincial public servants reported about a year ago on a very exciting economic development project for western Canada. They pointed out that the Government of Ontario presently buys about $1 billion worth of coal a year from the Americans. However, it is coal with a high sulphur content, it is dirty coal and it spews acid rain into the air. Ontario Hydro must reduce those emissions by 50 per cent by the year 1990. They have a choice. They can either
March 14, 1988

invest very heavily in expensive scrubbers and technologies to eliminate the sulphur content, or they can purchase western Canadian coal from the foothills of Alberta.
That would have enormous economic payoffs. There would be $6 billion or $7 billion of new capital investment and 20,000 to 30,000 new jobs, not only in the mines themselves but along the railroad lines from western Canada to the hydro plants in Ontario. That is an incredibly important regional development project for the West.
The key to making it work, as the task force reported, would be necessary freight rate subsidies of about $6 or $7 a tonne. No one should be frightened by that. We have been using freight rate subsidies in Canada since Confederation in order to compensate for our geography. There are freight rate programs in the Atlantic. Of course, the most important freight rate program is under the Western Grain Transportation Act, which subsidized the movement of grain by about $60 and $70 a tonne. Without that we would not be able to export our grain because we must send our wheat and barley along an extensive railway line.
The task force reported that the key to making it work is a freight rate program. That is a legitimate and interesting possibility for western Canadian development. It would involve $6 billion or $7 billion of investment and some 20,000 to 30,000 jobs.
While this would make for a useful debate for Canadians, we will no longer have the right to make that decision on the day the trade agreement the Prime Minister has signed comes into effect. Western Canadians will not be able to bring about that kind of program because the trade agreement would clearly eliminate the possibility of a new freight rate subsidy for the movement of western coal. Once the agreement is signed, would the Americans watch a $1 billion a year purchase be replaced by western Canadian coal without kicking up a fuss or threatening to abrogate the agreement because it betrays the principles of national treatment? Would they not undertake trade actions against this?
The Member from Alberta should have a strong interest in the development of western Canadian coal. If he supports that trade agreement he will be rejecting one of the most important potential projects for western Canadian economic development in this generation. How can he say that this will be a great boon for western Canada when it will be eliminating some of the major projects that we would have.
That is not the only example. Mr. Archie McLean, VicePresident of McCain's Food, who is a Conservative by his own admission, wrote to the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney). He said that while he is a hard core Conservative, she is dead wrong when it comes to the trade agreement. The food processing industry is an essential part of the food chain in Canada and an essential industry in western Canada. Mr. McLean said that as a Canadian food processor he has the choice either to shut down his plants in Canada or move south.
Western Canada bases a large part of its industry on agriculture and food processing. That industry is being put into jeopardy, and let me give an example of why. McCain's has a large plant in Portage la Prairie where it makes frozen French fries. They buy potatoes from the farmers of the Portage Interlake district of Manitoba for about $120 a tonne. This is a very important source of supply for those farmers. However, McCains can get the same potatoes in Idaho for $93 a tonne. Mr. McLean suggests that his next plant would be located where the input costs are lower. The same example applies to other vegetables, chickens and other products.
Madam Speaker, I hope I will be able to continue after Question Period and edify the House as to why the trade agreement is a disaster for western Canada.

subsubtopic: THE LATE JUDGE MARCEL CRETE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity to pay a last tribute to a great Canadian, the Hon. Marcel Crete, Chief Justice of the Quebec Court of Appeal, who died Friday night in Montreal. We were very sad at the news of his death. Judge Crete contributed greatly to the development of law in Quebec.
Born in La Tuque, the Chief Justice went to school in Grand-Mere and Trois-Rivieres before going to Laval University. He was called to the bar in 1937 and studied at Osgoode Hall in Toronto.
The Chief Justice practised law in Grand-Mere for 29 years before being appointed to the Superior Court of Trois-Rivieres in September 1966. He was subsequently appointed to the highest court in the province, the Quebec Court of Appeal, in January 1972. Finally, in 1980 he became Chief Justice.
Respected by his colleagues and friends, Judge Marcel Crete was a man of integrity and principle. In 1986, he was awarded the Medaille du Barreau in recognition of his great legal skills and commitment to the community.

March 14, 1988
The death of Chief Justic Marcel Crete is a great loss to us all. I am sure my colleagues in the House share my grief and will want to join me in extending our sincere condolences to his family and friends.

subsubtopic: CHARTERED BANKS-SUPPORT FOR REFUSAL OF APPLICATION TO SELL LIFE INSURANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadian banks are still asking for permission to get into the life insurance business but our Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is right in not allowing Canadian banks to sell life insurance.
There has been little or no movement from banks to stop the petty charges that are a burden to their customers. The banks have not stopped charging customers for services they did not explain to customers when their accounts were opened, nor do they feel they have to give an explanation or proof of work done when money is taken out of a customer's account without the customer's knowledge.
Can you imagine the games, Mr. Speaker, that could be played with insurance? I have already heard of one banking institution which refused to pay an insured loan because it claimed the insured customer knew of his health condition when the loan was taken out. I agree with the Minister.

subsubtopic: SINKING OF NOVA SCOTIAN FISHING VESSEL WITH LOSS OF LIVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all Members will want to express sympathy to the community of Sambro, Nova Scotia, for the apparent loss of a 68-foot wooden vessel, Bonnie Lou II, and a crew of five young men. The subsequent search and rescue attempt took place in very heavy seas under adverse weather conditions, once again showing the danger and difficulty of a fishing occupation in Canada.
In October the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) released the Coast Guard Study into Fishing Vessel Safety. Much attention was given to the placement of blame on those who fish for a living and the way they practise their trade, suggesting that fishermen were careless.
There are a number of issues that need to be addressed by the Minister. First, mandatory use of EPRBs aboard fishing vessels would ensure that distress signals can be monitored. Recently two resolutions were passed in the Nova Scotia
Legislature, supported by all Parties, calling upon the federal Government to establish a search and rescue base at Yarmouth for the South West Nova region. I urge that sympathy be followed by action so that the dangers inherent in this occupation can be reduced.

Mr. Speaker, on March 8 the Premier of Quebec, Mr. Robert Bourassa, announced that Quebec would start building new hydro-electric power stations this year.
Construction on three new stations at LG-1, Laforge and Brisay at James Bay, in the federal riding of Abitibi, at a cost of $7.5 billion during the next seven years, is a reassuring prospect for Quebecers, since it will create 40,000 jobs, involve major investments, and we will be able to export our surplus power to the United States.
Mr. Bourassa said that to him, letting Quebecers benefit from this natural resource was a tangible form of patriotism.
Mr. Speaker, it is a source of pride for Quebecers who believe in this great project and it is a source of great satisfaction for me as a former employee with technical surveys at Hydro-Quebec from 1965 to 1968.
Bravo, Mr. Bourassa, you are a great Quebecer!

subsubtopic: CREDIT CARD INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is just a year ago that the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs presented its report on credit card interest rates in Canada.
Contrary to speculation around the Hill, my broken wrist is not due to having my arm twisted by any credit card lobbyist.
I refer to the report because it is a demonstration of how Parliament can work for Canadian consumers. Since the report, interest rates on credit cards have been reduced, and there have been other gains made for consumers. But there is much yet to be done.

subsubtopic: CHERNOBYL NUCLEAR ACCIDENT-RADIATION LEVELS- INCIDENCE OF SICKNESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has now
been almost two years since the Chernobyl nuclear accident in

March 14, 1988
April, 1986. There has been some evidence that sickness from radioactive fall-out is on the increase in Ukraine. Malnutrition is also a problem. Some residents of the Ukraine are unable to secure food from uncontaminated areas and are afraid to use local meat or milk.
The Soviet news agency, Tass, reported in July, 1987, that almost 75 per cent of the land around Chernobyl has been recultivated. Some 14 settlements that were evacuated at the time of the accident have been resettled, while another 20 will soon follow. These measures may very well increase the numbers of people becoming sick because of exposure to radiation in the environment and in the food chain.
Granted that the Chernobyl reactor lacked the safety features of later models such as the CANDU, the public is still very concerned about the possibility of another nuclear accident.
Therefore, I urge the Government to support the work being done internationally in such areas as evaluating acceptable levels of radiation and forms of intervention, informing the public, ensuring prompt notification of accidents, and supporting a proposal by the OECD to require states to consult their neighbours before building nuclear power stations in frontier areas.

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF GIL SCOTT AS PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the struggle for equality for opportunity took another giant step forward last Saturday night at the Harry Jerome awards dinner in Toronto when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announced the appointment of Gil Scott as a Commissioner of the Public Service Commission of Canada, the first ever visible minority person to hold that position.
This, combined with the appointment of Lincoln Alexander, the first ever visible minority person to serve as Lieutenant-Governor; the appointment of Cal Best, the first ever visible minority person to serve as a Canadian Ambassador; the Employment Equity Act, and the Affirmative Action Program for visible minorities in the Public Service, all in just over three years, is a record of which the Prime Minister and the Government can be proud.
However, the struggle for equal opportunity is not over and, in the words of one young Harry Jerome award winner last Saturday night, "the future is now".

subsubtopic: COMPARISON OF CONDITIONS ON RESERVES AND IN METIS COMMUNITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this weekend I had an opportunity to tour some remote communities in the Churchill riding. I was depressed by the fact that after many years of both Liberal and Conservative regimes the people living on reserves do not have water systems, do not have sewage systems, do not have adequate housing, and do not have the same amount of money spent per capita on their young children for education.
At the same time I toured some of my Metis communities which in many cases have water and sewage systems, more money spent on education, and better housing programs.
I call upon the federal Government to live up to its responsibilities to provide native people not only of northern Manitoba but of the whole country with adequate systems of housing, of water, of sewage, and of education.
I am concerned about the seniors in my riding, but I am more concerned about the youth. To see three-year olds, four-year olds, and five-year olds living and growing up at the end of the 20th century and not to see any attempt by the federal Government to resolve the problems is a complete catastrophe and a national disgrace.

subsubtopic: ONTARIO-INCREASE IN PROVINCIAL DEFICIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is hard to believe, but the economic boom times in Ontario seem to be bringing about a spending binge by the provincial Liberals that would make even Pierre Elliott Trudeau blush.
David Peterson is throwing money in every direction, and the people continue to line up for more. They think that Santa Claus has come to town again.
Last year's newly discovered $1 billion is gone. Even with a 5.9 per cent spending increase, Ontario could have balanced its books this year. Instead, unprecedented spending has gobbled up that SI billion windfall, has increased the Ontario annual deficit again this year, and now the Premier is forecasting increased taxes.
What a pity that the federal Government continues to put the Trudeau mess in order but Ontario may not benefit as it begins borrowing itself into economic chaos.
The piper will have to be paid. How long will it be before someone else will have to be brought into Ontario, this time to fix up the David Peterson economic mess?
March 14, 1988

subsubtopic: CANADIAN INVESTOR PROGRAM-QUEBEC PRACTICE HALTED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Investor Program allowed individuals with a net worth of $500,000 to attain landed status if they invest $250,000 in a Canadian venture for three years.
Recently Quebec Immigration found a loophole whereby immigrant investors were being guaranteed their investments of $250,000 and received an annual interest rate of 3 per cent on the amount. This practice is contrary to the Immigration Act. The Minister, once informed of this practice, moved quickly and suspended the guarantees. He will not allow visas to be sold.
This scheme probably pre-empted the standard medical and security clearances, and it is not fair nor ethical for all those wishing to enter Canada. One immigration law must apply all across Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I indicated in the House the other day, the statement I made to the Canada-Israel Committee of course reflects the policy of the Government of Canada.
It is a policy that has been expressed, both in the letter which the Prime Minister wrote to the Prime Minister of Israel, in answers that I have given in the House of Commons, and in other positions the Government has taken.
The Hon. Member asks if the Prime Minister and I have discussed the matter in detail. He is asking the question: Did the Prime Minister of Canada and the Secretary of State for External Affairs discuss this speech word for word for word. Of course we did not. This Prime Minister of Canada has distinguished himself, among other ways, in encouraging his Ministers to exercise their responsibilities in their own fields and in their own Departments. I have done that. My colleague, the Minister of Finance, has done that. We do it with the full support of the Prime Minister of Canada.
The position of this country on issues relating to the Middle East is clear and is stated consistently by the Prime Minister, by myself, and by other spokesmen authorized to speak in that field for the Government.

Mr. Speaker, we know what the Secretary of State for External Affairs believes and what he has stated. My question was for the Prime Minister.
I want to repeat my question to the Prime Minister especially in light of his statement over the weekend about the remarks given by the Secretary of State. He said, "In speaking frankly you may question his words, but not his motives".
In this case the words are very important. They carry a great deal of meaning. I want to ask the Prime Minister explicitly: Does he question the words of the Secretary of State? Is he differing in any way from the remarks that were given in front of the Canada-Israel Committee last week? Does he have reservations and concerns about the kind of tone and nature of the remarks given by the Secretary of State?

Mr. Speaker, the question of my hon. friend is very surprising in light of a statement made this morning by his colleague, the Liberal Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East. He was quoted as saying this morning, referring to the NDP and Liberal speeches, and the Conservative speech given by the Secretary of State, that he read all of the speeches very thoroughly and it seems to him that there are no contradictions

March 14, 1988
Oral Questions
between any of the speeches and that the basic policy of the three Parties is the same. This was a statement made by the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East this morning. I wonder where my hon. friend is coming from.
With regard to my position, I have been on the record consistently. Perhaps I could quote something that I indicated on Saturday in Toronto. I said: "With regard to statements elsewhere, Mr. Clark has been a firm and a loyal friend of Israel throughout his entire political life. He spoke as a friend of Israel. "He spoke very much as a solid and a committed friend of Israel, trying to send out a message that a true friend can give,... that violence breeds violence and it would be most unfortunate if this gave rise to a situation which endangered this fragile democracy in the Middle East which is Israel and which we all support. Mr. Clark was attempting to be constructive to a friend ... He spoke with the conviction of someone who believes he could be frank because his friendship with Israel could never be question questioned."
The speech of the Secretary of State for External Affairs issued support for Israel, support for negotiated peace with the moderate Arab states. It called for restraint and an end to violence on both sides, and it spoke of his active support of the Shultz plan for a negotiated peace in the area. Surely no Member of the House would quarrel with any of those objectives.

Would the Prime Minister tell us whether the other countries of the Middle East which have been part of those hostilities, particularly Syria, share those same views? subtopic: GENERAL AGREEMENT ON TARIFFS AND TRADE
subsubtopic: PRELIMINARY RULING ON CANADIAN FISH EXPORTS
speechtext:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the Hon. Member would agree with me that we have taken a very important step forward. March 14, 1988

He has pointed out the problems he has seen in his constituency on the borderline between communities within the prescribed region for northern benefits and those that are just outside. subsubtopic: NORTHERN TAX ALLOWANCES-GEOGRAPHICAL DELINEATION OF AFFECTED COMMUNITIES
speechtext: What ought to be a most useful tax measure is in fact causing confusion, causing division, and causing a good deal of distress in many communities.

Mr. Speaker, will the Minister move quickly to amend these regulations and not pass on his responsibility to a commission or task force? We know what has to be done. Why do we not just get on and do it?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member says that he knows what has to be done. I suggest to him that that is a very facile way of dealing with the problem. If we knew what had to be done we would not be calling for the creation of this commission.
These borderlines between different communities are very difficult to address and very difficult to delineate because different sizes of communities, different geographical relationships and elements that are important in deciding whether a community should be inside or outside the prescribed areas are important questions upon which an objective person like a commissioner can give the Government some guidelines. Otherwise, I am sure that he or his colleagues would be the first to say that certain communities received special treatment because they have a Conservative Member of Parliament and another did not because it had a Liberal or NDP Member of Parliament. In fact, I believe that was already stated in this House last week.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance announced his intention to change the taxation policy for northern benefits almost two years ago. A year and one-half ago he announced the specifics of his intention. At that time I and others wrote him about the problems. One of his own Conservative Members rose in the House to say there was a problem.
Why is he only now setting up a commission to look into the problems with regard to this tax?

Mr. Speaker, since the time that the Hon. Member wrote we spent much effort in trying to find the proper resolution. It has been very difficult to do so and that is why we believe the best way to
proceed is to have an objective commissioner travel to different parts of the country and give us some advice on this.
I should point out to the Hon. Member that the value of this benefit is some $150 million to $175 million, which is considerably greater than the some $50 million under the remission order. Therefore, a number of communities have benefited by this and, as I indicated previously, pensioners, native people, small business people and others who did not have access to this benefit have access to it now.
We are trying to ensure that it is equitable, but the benefit has been provided to a much larger group of people. I do not think we should lose sight of that.

Mr. Speaker, there are people who can swim across to the American border who would benefit from this particular exclusion. There are others who live in the North who do not qualify. In the age of parliamentary reform and tax reform, why would the Minister not listen to Members of Parliament? Why did he not act when people were complaining about this problem? Since he refused to act, will he make whatever changes come about retroactive because there are people in the North, not only in Manitoba but in other parts of Canada, who are excluded and unfairly treated because he would not listen and act when he should have.
I think it is quite wrong to say that I have not listened.
You said no.
I have listened to a wide range of Members of Parliament.
You said no.

The Hon. Member cannot ask his question seriously if he has his mouth open during the time I am trying to answer. We believe that the best way to deal with this is through a commissioner. We feel that will lead to a more objective resolution for difficult problems.
He says there are many people in the North who are not receiving this benefit. I say to those people that nothing has been taken away from them. Many people in the North are now receiving this benefit for the first time.

speechtext: Order!

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS TO LEGISLATIVE COMMITTEE ON BILL C-72
speechtext:
The Hon. Member rises with respect to the appointments to a legislative committee. So that the public that is watching and listening to this will understand what this means, after a Bill has passed second reading it then goes in most cases to a legislative committee. Depending on the wish of all three Parties, the legislative committee can be of different sizes. The Hon. Member is rising on a question of privilege because he says that some groups in the country that are important in this matter do not have, I take it, a Member who sits specifically in a seat which represents their concerns. speechtext:
The Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) has raised a question which is clearly of very great importance to the Chair. Bill C-72, quite properly so, has gained a great deal of attention from all sides of the House. There have been different views as to the Bill itself.
What the Hon. Member is now asking the Chair to do is something that the Chair cannot do, that is, expand unilaterally the numbers on a committee, or for that matter determine the appointment of Hon. Members to the committee, which as I indicated a few minutes ago is the prerogative of each of the Parties.
It is true that the Chair, that is, myself, has not only the privilege but the obligation to appoint the chairperson of that committee. Hon. Members will know that I have exercised that prerogative, and I think properly so, by appointing my Deputy Speaker, who I think will not only be acceptable to all Members in the House but who has clearly demonstrated on many occasions his impartiality and his concern for both linguistic communities.
I am sorry to have to advise the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East that, despite the fact that he might very well have a complaint with his colleagues in his own Party, or his own Whip, or others in the Chamber, it is not a matter on which the Chair can intervene. difficulties in getting this committee struck. I shared with you in confidence some of my concerns about that, Mr. Speaker. I did not raise them in the House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext: When the House took recess at 1.14 p.m., the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) had the floor.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, just before I continue, I wonder whether the Chair could indicate how much time I have remaining.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext: Seven minutes.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, seven minutes will not do justice to the remarks I want to make, but I will do my best.
As I was pointing out before the luncheon break, the proposed trade agreement being negotiated when signed will have a devastating effect upon the western Canadian economy in a number of areas. I cited as evidence the representations of the food processing industry. It is also instructive to look at the kinds of concerns being raised by the agricultural community. The abandonment of the clear principle of subsidies on the transportation system, the surrender of that basic principle, will cause enormous consternation in the future. When we become involved in the negotiations at Geneva concerning agriculture, the precedent that the Government has now accepted and established in the Western Grain Transportation Act, which in fact is a trade related subsidy, will be used by other countries as a way to force the veto of that very essential means of development.
If we look at the fruit and vegetable industry, the whole development of the Fraser Valley in British Columbia will be put in jeopardy. The British Columbia Federation of Agriculture appeared before our task force just a few weeks ago and clearly enunciated major concerns that the horticultural industry of the province would be in jeopardy. It is also true for the vegetable industry of Manitoba with the problems being faced in that area.
The Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour) went to great length to indicate the bonanza which would be created in the petrochemical, oil, and gas industries-the energy field. The effect of the trade agreement on

March 14, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
the energy sector will be more serious than on any other sector. For example, the United States needs our energy resources. It has the biggest appetite for energy of any country in the world. Basically it is becoming a buyer's market. At the very moment when we know that the United States desperately needs our energy resources, what do we do? We fix a price. We do not go to a market price, or to allowing that kind of demand to set prices. The constraint is that if we raise prices for the Americans we would have to raise them for Canadian consumers. We will not be able to take full advantage of the opportunities created by the fact that it is now a buyer's market.
I submit that we are giving up one of the most competitive advantages of western Canada. Let us also consider the petrochemical field. How was it formed? How were various industries in Manitoba formed? They were formed by using energy as a competitive advantage. We gave a special price to those users, but we could no longer do that.
The trade agreement will substantially limit the major industrial advantage we have in terms of developing a new comparative arrangement vis-a-vis the United States. Where do we have an advantage over them? Is it in skilled manpower or resources? The Americans have those commodities. Increasingly our advantage is in cheaper energy resources. However, the Government is giving it up. The Government is surrendering it. It is abandoning the future of western Canada in utilizing hydroelectric power, natural gas, and petroleum to give Canadian industry a substantial advantage in competing with the Americans and competing world-wide. That totally denies logic and the opportunity for industry to grow in western Canada. We are the source blood of energy, whether it is hydroelectric power in British Columbia and Manitoba or natural gas in Alberta, British Columbia, and Saskatchewan. The fact is that that is the key to the future of the western Canadian economy. However, the Government has put a lock on it. It has put a fix on it. It has given away that opportunity.
The Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona attempted to justify the trade deal as being a great bonanza. The fact is that we will lose jobs in a number of existing industries. Also we are giving up a major competitive advantage in one of our most important industries. I submit that western Canada will be devastated in its opportunity and its potential. Whatever small amount of money will trickle in as a result of western diversification, it will be lost in comparison with the enormous subtraction that will take place as a consequence of the Government going ahead and ratifying the particular deal with the Americans.
That is the real story for western Canada. Contrary to the claims and promises, it will become an albatross around western Canada and a major deterrent to the development of new industrial and resource based industries in the West. That is the real tragedy, and the House should be debating the surrender and abandonment of the western Canadian economy by the Government.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to speak very briefly to a number of points which the Hon. Member raised. He told us that the Auto Pact was managed trade. Will he tell us when other than I believe in 1968, when any of the minimum production safeguards were used other than briefly in 1980 or 1981 when Chrysler was in difficulty. In fact, to all intents and purposes we have free trade in the auto industry. That is why Oshawa and southern Ontario is doing so well. In western Canada we are all delighted about that, but I do not think it is fair for the Member to pretend that the Auto Pact is not a free trade agreement. It is one that can be terminated on one year's notice by the Congress, whereas under the trade deal if Congress wants to kill the Auto Pact it will have to kill the entire trade agreement. In that sense it entrenches a very good thing for southern Ontario and parts of Quebec, and I am all for it.
The Member mentioned the use of high sulphur coal. I have looked into this matter. I share fully the concerns of my fellow western Canadian colleagues about the use of high sulphur coal. Perhaps the Hon. Member can do something with Premier Peterson about encouraging Ontario Hydro not to use high sulphur coal. I was told recently that in a few years when those contracts run out we will be able to move low sulphur western coal by pipeline through to Ontario Hydro. There will no need for a transportation subsidy. I assume the subsidy is what the Hon. Member is concerned about in the trade agreement.
The Hon. Member mentioned food processing. I tried over the lunch hour to get a list of the organizations in western Canada in favour of the trade agreement but three or four provincial Governments are in favour, presumably four on April 26 with Manitoba, the Canada West Foundation, the C. D. Howe Institute, the Canadian Cattlemen and Milton Harris. I remind the Hon. Member that Mr. Harris is president of the Harris steel group. He said he will abandon his lifelong Liberal membership because he feels so strongly that this agreement is good for the steel industry across Canada. The grain and oil seed sector will benefit, the lumber industry will benefit. Who in western Canada other than the Hon. Member and the outgoing dead or dying Government of Manitoba and Mel Hurtig, a friend of mine in Edmonton, agrees with the Hon. Member on this?
The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) referred to the energy agreement. I have a paper here by Professor Brian Scarfe of the University of Alberta on the trade agreement. Professor Scarfe certainly thinks, as do most people in the energy industry in Calgary, Edmonton, Saskatoon and everywhere else, that the agreement will do a great deal to help create jobs and keep jobs in the energy industry. Perhaps the Member might like to deal with some of those points, or perhaps his friend, the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), might do it for him.
March 14, 1988

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first let me comment on the Auto Pact. It is instructive that Victor Lomo who represents the Auto Pacts Manufacturers of Canada, a most important industrial based group, has said he is against this agreement because it will devastate the auto parts industry of Ontario. He appeared before a Liberal trade task force about four weeks ago. I will be glad to send the Hon. Member the comments of Mr. Lomo.
Second, the Member raises the question about the coal project. The fact is, and I use it as illustration, that the choice and option for Canadians to use a form of subsidy for regional development is now constrained by this trade agreement. We know that all kinds of projects in the future will require that kind of investment in the infrastructure of western Canada because of our geography and climate. In fact, the restraint and inhibition put on developing the western coal project as it now stands is one of the most serious and clear examples of how we put a straitjacket on regional development for western Canada from a federal level.
Third, who supports the trade deal? We finished a series of hearings across the West. I can name groups. There are the data processors, a number of agricultural groups, a number of social organizations and coalitions. If the Hon. Member looked at the surveys he will see that one was just conducted in British Columbia last week which pointed out that 60 per cent of the people want an election to determine this matter and a large percentage of women are against it.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext: Eighty per cent think that Americans will benefit.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext:
And 80 per cent think the Americans will benefit. I suggest the Hon. Member should consult western Canadians. There are as many people concerned about the trade deal as are in favour of it. There are many industrial groups which know they will be seriously affected. The truckers, the furniture manufacturers, the food processors, the data processors and people in the high technology industries all realize that they have been put in jeopardy.
The Hon. Member mentions lumber. This agreement entrenches an $800 million tax on the Canadian lumber industry. It requires us to impose a penalty on ourselves and it has not been negotiated away. Similarly, the Government gave away in the agreement the right of the fish processing industry to use an export tax to protect processing industries on the West Coast and on the East Coast. The Government had an opportunity to gain an advantage for western Canadians but the Government gave it away. The Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour) and other Members from western Canada have not subjected the deal to the kind of clear analysis required for its economic impact. I submit to this House that if Members look at this in an honest way and look at the figures of the Government's own analysis, western Canada ends up the economic loser under the Mulroney trade deal.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wish to ask the Member who was at one time a Cabinet Minister in the Liberal Government what happened to the western development fund. In doing so, I would like to quote from western Canadian newspapers including The Winnipeg Free Press. On October 29, 1980 there is a picture of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) when he was a Cabinet Minister talking about this bonus to Manitoba and speaking about the western development fund of $4 billion which will be used to help the western economy diversify. The article goes on to talk about the types of initiatives that should take place. That was October, 1980.
In January, 1981 a Saskatchewan paper had an article saying that the province is in the dark concerning the western development fund.
Going a bit further, in May, 1981 there is an article in The Financial Post about the western development fund saying that the $4 billion has been put on ice.
In June, 1981 we have the person who normally occupies the Chair, the Hon. Member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) asking what has happened to the western development fund. The Hon. Member from Winnipeg-Fort Garry says "It is cynical to say that the western development fund has disappeared or that it is not going to be used.
I can go on month after month, year after year, but since the Member was the man who was supposed to be, to use the quote from The Winnipeg Free Press, "parcelling out the money to western Canada", can he explain to this House what happened to that promise? Here we are in 1988 four years after his Party left, so we cannot blame him for the problems of the last four years, but what happened in 1980? What happened in 1981? What happened in 1982? What happened in 1983? And what happened before September 4, 1984?
I know the Member from Winnipeg-Fort Garry knows there was high unemployment, that the agricultural industry was suffering, that the provinces at that time were quite willing to participate in a western development fund. I do not want to cut the Member off, but I do want to have a chance to answer the question. It seems to me that the $4 billion was a phantom fund. Certainly some money was spent in western Canada but all the hype, the publicity, the PR and all the promises disappeared. Since the Member was the person who was supposed to be parcelling out the money, perhaps he can explain, four years after he is no longer a Minister, what happened to the dollars?

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am surprised the Hon. Member who comes from western Canada is so totally and absolutely ignorant about what did happen to it. I would have thought a Member serving his constituents would have spent a little time determining the facts. They are very simple.
Of the $4 billion, $3.5 billion was spent on modernizing the railway system of western Canada. That was based upon consultation with the provinces, with the industry and with the

March 14, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
sector. The conclusion was very clear. But the single most important investment required was the total modernization of the railway system. We could not move the products from his riding to ports with the deterioration that was going on in the railway system. The Government of Canada, through the western cabinet committee, made a clear decision to invest $3.5 billion in the modernization of railways. That has taken place and is ongoing at the present time.
1 am really surprised that the Elon. Member does not know that the rest of the money was established as part of a native economic development fund, setting up a bank to allow native groups across western Canada to start their own businesses and self-development projects, many of which are now working. The fact that an Hon. Member with a large native population in his riding does not know about that simply shows that he has not been doing his homework.
While we are on the subject, I would simply point out that in addition to those two major investments, the previous Government also put $1.2 billion into a special regional allocation of which over $550 million was spent in my home Province of Manitoba. That was matched by private sector and provincial moneys, so in fact an additional $2.1 billion was spent by 1984 on a whole range of projects for the development of western Canada.
I would be glad to elaborate on this some more if the Hon. Member really wants to know. I am totally surprised that he would not know by this time, four years later, what an important and effective investment we made in the West.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak on debate today, particularly because in the last couple of weeks,
I have seen this particular fund in action. I am quite excited about the projects that are being considered or have been approved by the fund.
We all know that the fund was established because western Canada is a very unique region and its resources of mining, fishing and agriculture are susceptible to international markets. As the market falls internationally, there is a bust and if there are good prices on those commodities, there is a boom. Our Government has said that that is not satisfactory, that we have to diversify the West. Not only that, the Government has said that westerners should say what they want. The people and the businesses of western Canada should have input.
The Government has assigned a western cabinet Minister the responsibility for the western diversification fund. A Deputy Minister is located in western Canada and now western Canadians are making the decisions in Edmonton, a centre of western Canada.
I would like to tell Hon. Members of one of the projects I had an opportunity to announce in my riding in Winnipeg last
week, and that is the Elder's Aquafarm. I think this is a very unique project. There was a malting plant right in the centre of Winnipeg that was not being utilized any longer for environmental reasons. The Elder's Grain Company came up with the idea of converting the tanks used for malting into fish tanks. The company started to proceed with this project and it will cost in excess of some $2 million to achieve it. The interesting part is that there are now fish being raised economically in the centre of Winnipeg. Profits will be made by this private company in association with the western diversification fund.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext: Winnipeg goldeye?

speechtext:
No, it is not Winnipeg goldeye. The company is raising Arctic char and trout. They anticipate that within a couple of years, over one million pounds of pan-sized fish will be produced by this plant to be sold in western Canada and the United States. This has come about because of the diversification fund which has assisted the company to some degree. I might add that the fund has made a loan that the company will be paying back, it was not an outright grant. This project will create 15 jobs.
Another project the western diversification office is looking at is one which I think is very interesting, namely, a robotics paint shop for commercial aeroplanes. Aeroplanes could be automatically painted by robots without any human contact with the fumes and the deadly gases. The company that is dealing with the western diversification office on this has already designed a robotic shop for the CN Railway yards in Transcona, and that has been a success. The company can now take this knowledge and software and develop it not only in Manitoba but in Saskatchewan. The company would then develop through private enterprise this paint shop for aeroplanes located in Winnipeg which will create many, many jobs. These are the kinds of projects this fund is attracting.
Another area that is being attracted by the fund is the geriatric health field. A company is interested in developing and expanding its location with a product developed in Europe. This company wants to bring this technology to western Canada and is talking about doubling the size of the plant. It is talking about 50 jobs. This is what the diversification fund is doing in my area, and I am sure this is happening in Saskatchewan and elsewhere as well. Our Government believes that westerners should have a chance at these kinds of projects.
Just to give Hon. Members an idea of the interest of the Opposition in this, members of the NDP voted against providing the western diversification fund with an initial $100 million, and they also voted against the $127 million for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. We know what they are interested in.
Liberal Members talk about being interested in diversification in the West. 1 would like to tell Hon. Members about the voting record of Liberal Members. That pattern of voting would turn down the economy of western Canada even further than it would have gone if they had stayed in Government.
March 14, 1988

We know how important the energy sector is for western Canada. In the first session, the Liberals voted against the repeal of the disastrous National Energy Program, including changes to the royalty regime. They voted against the repeal of the incremental oil revenue tax in that first session.
The Liberals voted against competition in air and rail transportation. We all know that transportation plays a very important part in the economy of the western provinces. Our goods must be transported across such a large area. The Liberals voted against increased competition in transportation which would mean lower transportation rates.
The agricultural sector is a very important part of the economy of western Canada as well. The Liberals voted against the $500,000 capital gains tax exemption for Canadian farmers and so did the NDP. They do not realize that farms are the pension plans of farming families. If farmers were taxed on capital gains, they would not find it worth their while to sell the farms. There would not be a changeover within a family unit or within the sector, and we need new blood in the farming community.
The Liberals also voted against the expenditure of $92 million for drought relief for western farmers, Bill C-101, in the first session. This is the kind of interest members of the Liberal Party have in western Canada. No wonder they talk negatively about the western diversification fund. It is good for western Canada, and it would appear from their voting record that they are not interested in western Canada.
The Liberals voted against giving the Canadian Wheat Board $200 million to meet its deficit, Bill C-47 in the second session. Again, they were not interested in western Canada. The Liberals voted against increased foreign investment through the creation of Investment Canada and the dismantling of FIR A in the first session. We know how important foreign investment is. Foreign investment is now encouraged to come to Canada.
The project to which I referred earlier dealing with geriatric health involves foreign investment which is willing to invest and expand in Winnipeg and bring technology with it. I am sure it would not be interested in doing that if FIRA were still in place. That is the kind of attitude members of the Opposition have toward diversification. We are fortunate to some degree in Manitoba that we are probably more diversified than most western provinces. Yet even then, we are still at the mercy of international wheat prices.
We as a Government saw fit to support strongly the farm community in its time of need over the past two years. We injected billions of dollars into that sector, not only in western Canada but in all of Canada, to make it stay alive. We also made sure the towns and communities dependent upon the industry stayed alive.

Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Minaker), about the payroll tax in Manitoba, the Hon. Member absolutely refused to deal with it. Do you know why? Member to slam the New Democrats on something that is, according to the Hon. Member, very unpopular in Manitoba. Yet the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James does not want to be in the position of attacking his former cabinet colleague in Manitoba, Mr. Filmon, and avoids the question.
This is an opportunity for me to speak on the issues on which the Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Minaker) is afraid to speak. However, before I talk about this particular problem I want to add to the comments that I made when the
Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James spoke earlier. We are now in a situation similar to that in October, 1980 when the then Minister of Finance, Mr. MacEachen, who is now in the other place, declared that there was going to be $4 billion for a western development fund. We waited through the rest of 1980, through 1981, through 1982, through 1983, and until the Liberals were defeated in 1984, and the western development fund did not come into being.
The Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) said that a lot of money was spent on transportation and the rest was spent on native economic development. Yes, there was money spent on western transportation and there was money committed for native economic development, money that was never spent. The former Minister, the Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry, had talked about a western development fund for diversifying the West, a fund which would create new industries in the West and would help all parts of the West to have industrial development. That money never came. In the West we started calling it the phantom fund.
We can understand the nervousness of the Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry because, as I said earlier, he was the Minister in the Liberal regime and was supposed to parcel out the money. He travelled to B.C., Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba talking about how valuable this $4 billion would be for the West. We are still waiting. It never happened. That was a broken promise of the Liberals. That is the sort of thing which makes people in western Canada upset about what happens on this Hill.
In 1980 and 1981 people in the West thought the Government was giving them the shaft. In October, 1980, there was a sense that we had finally been recognized as a region of Canada which would no longer only be involved in growing wheat and exporting natural resources. The talk about a $4 billion western development fund gave a lot of hope to people in the West. As time passed, that hope was taken away and we saw that nothing was going to happen. First there was a retreat. It was no longer $4 billion but became $2 billion. It was no longer to diversify the West, it was, as the Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry just said, to help maintain the transportation system in the West. We were not told the truth, and every time a cabinet Minister stood up we found out that there was less and less money for the West and that the money would be used for fewer and fewer programs.
Here we are, four years after the defeat of the Liberals, with another Government, this Government has less than 18 months left in its term of office and last year it promised a western diversification fund. Legislation is before a committee of this House at this time and nothing has happened. People in the West are again asking what is going on. They were promised the money and the provinces have put forward proposals, but the Government did not even introduce the legislation into the House until just over a month ago.
We in the West feel that we are again being given more cynical political promises. We went through that with the

former Liberal Government. The Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry never defended the West, and his answers in the House today proved that the western development fund was a myth.

We do not want to go back to the days of the Right Hon. Member for Yellow-head (Mr. Clark) where interest rates were at 18 per cent, 19 per cent and 20 per cent. What my riding association is saying is that there are other things to consider than what the Chairman of the Bank of Canada thinks. He may be concerned about inflation, which tends to be the main preoccupation of the Bank of Canada, but there are people in the regions, on farms, people in small business, men and women right across this country, who are very concerned about keeping their businesses operating and interest rates have killed and maimed many small businesses.
Despite the implications made by the Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona, I think a resolution saying we should look at controlling interest rates is a damn good thing for this country.
Second, the Hon. Member referred to controlling the price of fossil fuels. Let me explain why that resolution was introduced in 1985. For his benefit, I will point out that I represent
Western Economic Diversification Act
a northern riding where most of the communities are 300, 400, 500 or 600 miles north of the City of Winnipeg. The people in my riding buy gasoline just as do people right across this country. However, they noticed that if they drive to a community to the south, they pay 36 cents a litre for gas, if they go 50 miles north, they pay 40 cents a litre for gas. If they go 150 miles north, they pay 50 cents a litre for gas, and if they go further north they pay more than that. The City of Thompson, Manitoba decided to abandon the commercial dealerships. It decided not to pay those high prices that Esso, Texaco or Shell insisted on. The people of that city were going to put together a gas co-op. The community of Thompson discovered they could sell gas for 10 cents a litre less than the commercial operators were charging. The City of Thompson could do that quite easily because it had a fairly large population. It had a population of 14,000 people and all of them wanted to set up their own gas co-op and be able to sell gas for a lot less. However, that is not so easy for the people in smaller towns.
The people in smaller towns went to Shell and to the other companies and told them that Thompson, Manitoba, 250 miles away, was selling gas for 6 cents, 7 cents or 8 cents a litre less than people were paying in The Pas or in some of the other communities. They wanted to know why. We have an oligarchy in this country which basically controls the wholesale distribution and price of gas.
I notice that the Member who asked the question has disappeared. I think the answer overwhelmed him. The northern communities realized they were not in a situation where there was free enterprise and competition. They were being told by the local dealer that he would love to sell gas to them at a cheaper price but he could not because Shell and the other gas companies would not let him. So the people in my riding said we should have some system put in place which allowed for the freight cost into the North because it does cost more when you ship oil and gas to the North. They found out that they could move gas 450 miles into Thompson and still sell it for 10 cents a litre less than what the private enterprise competition was charging.
I can understand why the people in my riding put forward a resolution saying, yes, we should do something to regulate fossil fuel prices so that people do not get ripped off, and I support the people in my riding association who put that forward. I suspect that most of the people in a producing province and in a producing city such as Alberta would also support the same type of resolution.

March 14, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext:
It seemed as if we were getting into the preliminary skirmishes, but then of course we do not know who the players are and that may be premature.
It has been stated by Members on both sides of the House that others have talked about western diversification, but it is only now and only recently that something substantial is being done about it. I can recall attending a national industry meeting in Winnipeg in April, 1982, and having the Prime Minister of the day, the Right Hon. Pierre Elliott Trudeau, speak on his vision of western Canada. Those who were not amused were bemused. It seemed to be an awakening on the road to Damascus on the part of this remarkable Canadian. Of course, as the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) has so aptly put it, that was the beginning and the end of it. There was double-tracking, which I think was credited to the Liberals' account. But there was more double-talking than there was double-tracking.
We are now doing something about it. I should point out that the Government did not wait until the legislation appeared in the House to act on western diversification. In fact, not long after the announcement was made in Edmonton on August 4, 1987, applications began to flood in. In fact, there was so much interest and so much pre-activity shown with respect to the issue of western diversification that I am told there was a considerable amount of staff burn-out and staff turnover in the beginning weeks.
Frankly, while it was known that there was western entrepreneurial genius and outstanding ideas within western Canada, no one quite estimated the quality, depth and volume of that activity. It is now six months since the initiative was announced. I am happy to report that based on my experience it is operating very well. The office in Edmonton is running well. Many projects have been approved or are in the final assessment phase. Others, for various reasons, have been sent back for modification or, in fact, have been rejected for not meeting the criteria. I hope that there will be some time to touch upon those criteria.
There are quite a few distinguishing characteristics of the western diversification initiative that set it apart from previous initiatives of previous Governments and, indeed, initiatives of provincial Governments, in that it is designed to top up, to facilitate, to lever, to be last dollar in. In other words, it is the final achiever of projects that are otherwise worthy.
I could touch on one or two examples of initiatives that went through prior to the establishment of western diversification. I think of the western transportation diversification fund, which was a last gasp effort of the previous Government but which we have acted on.
I point out that in the cultural field, in which I have more than a passing interest, I had the privilege of participating just last Tuesday at the ribbon-cutting of a new $7 million motion picture production studio in my constituency which was enabled in part through a grant from WTID.
This is quite a departure in philosophy from that of previous Governments, as I have mentioned. We have stopped the process of throwing dollars at the sunset. That is a significant departure. If there is one thing which rankles the populace, it
is the idea of keeping alive an industry which should not be kept alive through government intervention. Indeed, a great deal of research, planning and consultation went into the establishment of the western diversification fund and the western diversification office. At the request of at least two provincial Governments the announcement of the initiative was delayed on two occasions so that the provincial Governments could have their proper input. I know that that occurred. I know that the initiative will succeed with greater efficacy because of that consultation and that input.
There are a good many examples of value added in the traditional fields of oil and gas and agriculture in my own Province of Alberta which had been enhanced or were in the process of being enhanced. There are a great many others in the process. But it is in the field of research and technology that I think we can take greatest pride in some of the achievements that have already gone ahead in the Province of Alberta.
Some of these are tangential to western diversification, within the umbrella of the initiative that is, and others are directly within the umbrella. For example, there was established in April of 1986 the Canada-Alberta subsidiary agreement on northern development, a $40 million program offering assistance in three key areas: expanded diversity of economic development in the North; assistance for northern residents to develop and access employment opportunities; and facilitation of the development of community and regional infrastructure in order to improve the long-term viability of business and industrial initiatives.
As you are well aware, Madam Speaker, our Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) chairs a committee which is instrumental in striving to bring western Canadian low-sulphur coal to Ontario for the use of Ontario Hydro. The committee is chaired by the Deputy Prime Minister and consists of Premiers Getty, Vander Zalm, Devine and Peterson. The objective is to improve the economic attractiveness of western Canadian coal so that Ontario coal users will make commercial decisions to increase their use of Canadian coal.
As well, there have been a number of initiatives undertaken by the Government of Alberta which is pushing forward high technology and research at the Alberta Microelectronics Centre, a non-profit organization located at the University of Alberta and the University of Calgary. The fabrication facility is in the northern city. The design facility is in the Stampede city. That centre will assist Alberta's growing electronics industry with the design and manufacture of leading-edge products which can be marketed worldwide. The Government of Alberta, I am happy to note, has contributed $14 million over three years for the centre starting in 1985.
The Alberta Laser Institute, which many of my colleagues are following with considerable interest, was established to work closely with private sector companies to transfer technology involving materials processing, laser sensors and the medical and electronic application of lasers to improve productivity, competitiveness and new product development. Again, I congratulate the Government of Alberta for contributing $5 million over five years.
March 14, 1988

So far there have been two major announcements under western diversification within the Province of Alberta. There was the $9.5 million participation in Daishowa Canada Limited, which will construct a major greenfield bleached kraft pulpmill near Peace River. That mill will cost more than $500 million and will create 630 mill and woodland jobs and 1,260 indirect jobs. The provincial Government is co-operating by assisting with rail and road access and other infrastructure.
This mill is unique because it is based on the use of aspen, or, as we used to call it, poplar, which is in some of our Alberta forests and which is certainly regarded by Alberta homesteaders and those who are trying to grow gardens as something of a weed. But it is now being put to proper use. I know that the Minister of State for Forestry and Mines (Mr. Merrithew) has been very much involved in the encouragement and the development of research in the use of aspen, which is no longer a weed but a distinct asset.
I had the opportunity just two weeks ago to tour a facility in the constituency of my friend, the Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour). The proprietor of the business happens to be a resident of my constituency. This is typical of the kind of world-scale research that is going on in the Province of Alberta, which will overcome the great handicap of distance and absence of markets which has plagued and hindered the diversification of the western economy heretofore. This particular facility is owned by local interests and collaborates with Japanese interests. It is known as Synphar Chemicals and is associated with the Taiho conglomerate of Japan. The work in which they are engaged relates to the extraction of natural compounds from plants and exotic seeds to substitute for the worrisome products derived from coal tar, which are used extensively in cosmetics and are unfortunately used in some food additives.
This research is going forward. At the end of the tour I said to the proprietor: "Are you looking for something from the Government?" He said: "No, Sir, we are not. We are going to do it on our own". I am happy to say that there are some situations which do not require government intervention. However, I am happy to say that western diversification will assist those who do, where it is critical to the success or failure of the venture.
Other work done by Norac Technologies Inc. relates to the extraction of natural compounds from plants and exotic seeds to substitute for the worrisome products derived from coal tar, which are used extensively in cosmetics and are unfortunately used in some food additives.
I was a little perturbed to hear the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) criticizing a distinguished public servant, the Deputy Minister who, by the way, is designated to reside in Edmonton. I think it is unique in Canadian legislation that the head office of an authority would be established outside the national capital region. Perhaps the Atlantic authority has a similar designation in its legislation. The Deputy Minister in question, to whom the Hon. Member for Churchill referred, I am happy to say is-and this is not his
Western Economic Diversification Act
only qualification for the job-a resident of the constituency of Edmonton South. I found that he and his staff have been exceedingly helpful, despite the tremendous volume of work they must do in sorting and assessing various proposals. They have been extremely helpful when my colleagues and I have been asked to refer to the office to determine the status of any particular project.
The people in the WDO office work long hours. They are committed to the success of western diversification. They are co-operative with provincial officials and with those who bring forward proposals.
I wish to touch on another role of the western diversification initiative, that is, the path-finding role. There are many other government programs which can be made applicable to our western situation. I am pleased that the WDO in Edmonton- and I am sure it is the same in the other offices across western Canada-has the capability of seeking out government programs, be they in the cultural field, telecommunications, agriculture, or whatever application, and of bringing the proposers and the doers together.
I mentioned that heretofore there have been two major announcements under WDO in the Province of Alberta. I touched briefly on the Daishowa project, which was announced on February 8 in a joint announcement by the federal and provincial Governments and the Japanese-based company.
In addition, I should like to take a moment or two of the time of the House to touch on the Centre for Frontier Engineering Research. It was my privilege to have worked with the project since the fall of 1984 to try to assist in bringing it to fruition. It is a remarkable institute. The concept of the Centre for Frontier Energy Research is a dual one. The interest in frontier engineering research is reflected in an industry-driven program aimed at materials design and constructed for Arctic and offshore energy development. The commitment which the centre has made to technological frontiers can be seen in its program of ground-breaking research focused on conventional, heavy oil, and oil sands operations.
The areas of research are two-offshore structures and down hole tubular systems. In addition, the Centre for Frontier Energy Research has a mandate including a commitment to networking, the movement of current technical information through industry. CFER Atlantic operating out of the technical university of Nova Scotia has also been developing well. The proposed laboratories are now properly funded and are proceeding well under the construction program that was laid out for them when the project was announced on December 22, 1987.
The joint federal-provincial commitment is $18 million. The federal Government will provide a $7.75 million capital contribution, and $1 million of that will be matched by CFER through industry supporters. The Alberta Government will provide a total of $6.75 million, which includes a $4.5 million capital grant, $1.25 million toward operating funds through to 1993, and a $1 million maximum interest subsidy. The province will also provide a loan guarantee of up to $5 million.

March 14, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
In the words of the Deputy Prime Minister who participated in the announcement, the facility will increase Canada's competitiveness in world markets and increase opportunities for Canadian engineering firms to compete on a worldwide basis. The engineering profession, the consulting industry in the Province of Alberta, was decimated through the depression of the early 1980s. We were at risk of losing the critical core of that profession, a profession truly in the forefront of world competence in the areas of civil engineering, petroleum engineering, and soil mechanics. Institutes such as the Centre for Frontier Engineering Research and others to come will do a great deal to provide a sea anchor to guard against that loss of competence and that loss of a critical mass.
I was pleased to note, at the announcement of the establishment of CFER, that the frontiers are not limited to our western and northern frontiers and that indeed there is an Atlantic dimension to the capability of the institute.
I want to dwell for just a moment on one or two aspects of the western diversification project so that there is some clarity as to what kind of assistance is available and what kind of projects are to be funded. One key feature is that service industries and resource-related industries are eligible for funding. The definition of who may apply has been expanded to include non-profit business organizations.
Examples of the kinds of projects which will be considered for funding-and I stress the word "considered"-are those in the general area of business projects or activities that would involve the initiation, promotion, or expansion of enterprises.
In addition, projects which contribute to the enhancement of the business climate or the development of business infrastructure will be considered, as will proposals for the modernization or expansion of existing industrial facilities.
I have dwelt at some length on research and development, another prime area of interest of the western diversification initiative. Projects involving systems or software development, new product identification, and the development of productivity improvement will be eligible as well.
We also have an eye to the export opportunities of the nation. Projects and activities with the capability of market development, whether it be domestic or international, fall within the terms of reference of the proposals.
Of course there are certain kinds of enterprises which are not eligible. Briefly, in the time remaining, I should caution that the program will not fund projects where the economic or employment benefits would apply primarily outside the western provinces. Projects designed to replace existing capital or operating requirements of government Departments of any of the three levels of government are not eligible for support. The program will not assist projects designed to create municipal infrastructure or foster urban redevelopment. In the case of commercial or industrial projects, the program cannot
support proposals where the applicant's net equity position is unreasonably low.
I appreciate this opportunity to touch on some aspects of western diversification. I, for one, am delighted and proud that the Government of the day has seen fit to bring in this Bill.
