subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to speak in this debate because the people of Manitoba welcome the proposal of the Conservative Government to establish this western diversification program. The Premier of Manitoba welcomed the agreement and indicated that Manitoba would co-operate fully and that Manitoba expected to get its fair share of the $1.2 billion which we were led to believe the program would have in the way of funds to be allocated over the next five years.
It is not surprising that people in Manitoba, as people in the four western provinces and in Atlantic Canada, were vitally interested in this proposal of the federal Government because people in western Canada and in Atlantic Canada have felt for a long time that they have been treated as second class citizens. The major benefits in this country of ours have gone to central Canada, to the people and the industries of Ontario and Quebec. It was felt that western Canada was looked upon as a resource hinterland for central Canada and that attempts to diversify the have-not regions of Canada have, to a large extent, failed. The first real thought given to this problem was that given by the Rowell-Sirois Commission in the 1930s which investigated these regional disparities and provided the rationale for the transfer of federal payments to the poorer provinces.
We have had a number of programs whose design and intent was to help the poorer provinces of this country move up and improve their economies so people in those areas would be provided with a better standard of living. We saw in the period of the former Conservative Government headed by Mr. Diefenbaker the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), a cabinet Minister at that time, who helped to establish the Agricultural Rehabilitation Development Act, ARDA, as it is known, in 1961. Its purpose was to take marginal farmland and marginal farming operations out of production and put them into other activities. In the Pearson and Trudeau Governments we had the development of programs such as DEVCO, DREE and DRIE. These have had some success, but to a large extent the have-not provinces of Canada and the people in those provinces still have a standard of living far lower than the people in the
March 14, 1988

Province of Ontario and, to a somewhat lesser extent, the Province of Quebec.
One inquiry into the effectiveness of DREE was conducted by the Economic Council of Canada in its 1977 study entitled Living Together. The Council found that DREE expenditures were significant enough to measure against other economic activity in only one region, that of Atlantic Canada. The council concluded that there was suggestive evidence that DREE had helped to provide half of the additional jobs required in the 1970-75 period caused by decreased outmigration and a reduction in the employment rate of about 1 per cent. In other provinces, such as Quebec, Saskatchewan and elsewhere, no reduction in disparity was measurable, most likely because the DREE expenditure was so small on a per capita basis as to be unmeasurable. It did not say that DREE was immune from criticism.
DREE began as a federal initiative, became a conduit for funds for provincial projects and then became a federal agency again. These projects led to political battles between the provinces and the federal Government as to which initiative should be taken. Of course, federal Governments, Liberal or Conservative, wanted a higher profile in western Canada. These arguments were not surprising.
There is a rationale and a convincing one for the need for joint federal-provincial initiatives if regional development plans are to be successful. Nowhere is this more true than in the Province of Manitoba where the provincial Government has taken a highly successful approach to encouraging job creation through its job fund activities. The result of those activities and because of the well diversified economy in Manitoba, the unemployment rates in Manitoba for the last five or six years have been continuously either the lowest of any province or the second lowest.
It is an unexpected but unfortunate fact that throughout the 1980s the mineral, grains and petroleum markets, so important in Saskatchewan and Alberta, were uniformly depressed. Yet, here is where we get to the problem that we see about the nature of this western diversification fund and the $1.2 billion which is to be allocated. We see that certain provinces, British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan have already been able to get approved, through this fund, tens of millions of dollars, while Manitoba has received virtually nothing. It is not surprising that there was a great deal of anger and hostility when the Conservative Member of Parliament, the Hon. Member for St. Boniface (Mr. Duguay), in explaining why Manitoba has so far received so little in approvals as compared to other provinces said, as reported in The Winnipeg Free Press, on February 29:
If you want to work co-operatively, it doesn't help to criticize. It isn't helpful
to engage in fed bashing.
Many Manitobans, and I think quite correctly, took exception and became angry by what they considered to be an attempt by the Member from St. Boniface-hopefully he was not speaking for the Conservative Government of Canada-to
Western Economic Diversification Act
blackmail the people of Manitoba and to blackmail the Government of Manitoba. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) reacted, and I believe he spoke for most Manitobans when he made a statement on March 1 in response as follows:
I ask Members opposite, was Manitoba supposed to be happy in the early stages of this Government about the cancellation of the VIA Rail shop and its subsequent downsizing? Were we supposed to be happy about the cancellation of the manufacturing and research technology centre? Were we supposed to be happy about the repeated attempts, now succeeding, to erode Winnipeg's role as a transportation sector in western Canada? Were we supposed to be happy about that abominable decision to award the CF-18 contract to Montreal?
Were we supposed to just lie down and be quiet about all these things? Is the Manitoba Government to give up its principles with respect to free trade and other issues on which it disagrees with the federal Government? Is this a counsel on the part of the Member for St. Boniface and the Government to a lack of integrity in the political process? Are we all supposed to suck up to the federal Government in order for our regions to be treated well? It is totally unacceptable.
That is how the people of Manitoba, regardless of political Party, feel, and it is the way they should feel.
Another suggestion was that because there was an NDP Government in Manitoba, which is supposedly opposed to the private sector, all the proposals it made, and it made many proposals, were laughed at because they totalled billions of dollars. Manitoba did not expect to get billions of dollars. However, what it did expect, and what Manitobans, regardless of Party, will demand, is its fair share of the funds which will be allocated through the western diversification fund.
Another suggestion was that the reason Manitoba did not get approval was that it had an NDP Government which was not friendly or supportive of the private sector and all the proposals made by Manitoba were for government programs. That is not true either and I want to put on the record a few examples of the proposals which were brought forward and which have not yet been approved by the Conservative Government.
In the City of Flin Flon in northwestern Manitoba, the Hudson Bay Mining & Smelting Co. has a copper smelter and a zinc refinery. That company has been operating in Flin Flon for more than 50 years. It provides direct employment for over 2,000 workers in Flin Flon, Leaf Rapids and Snow Lake, Manitoba, and Creighton, Saskatchewan. That plant needs major modernization so that it can be more productive and competitive with other operations in other countries and so that it can meet the new environmental standards which have been set. We are talking about a $ 100-million modernization program. The Government of Manitoba expects the entire cost of that modernization to come from the federal Government through the western diversification fund, and this is a project which would meet any criteria which any Government would set.
There was a proposal for an agricultural biotechnology and training consortium made by the University of Manitoba, the

March 14, 1988
Canada Pension Plan
Brandon University and the Assiniboine Community College, in co-operation with agricultural organizations and the private sector, and I emphasize the private sector. This proposal is to set up a consortium to focus on developing applications in agricultural biotechnology and providing agricultural management training.
One does not have to be an expert and read technical journals, one need only read The New York Times, Time magazine, Newsweek or any of the financial newspapers published in Canada to know that almost every week new discoveries are made in the field of agriculture so that tomatoes, potatoes or the like will be made resistant to the pests which attack them. Canada is lagging very seriously behind in research in this area.
A proposal came from the Government of Manitoba to set up a biotechnology and training consortium, and given the difficulties western Canadian farmers are having competing for the sale of grain and other products with countries which subsidize very heavily their agricultural industries, the management abilities of Manitoba farmers are more and more important than ever. This consortium would help with that, but again there has been no response from the federal Government.
A rural industrial project was proposed by the Manitoba Government to its federal counterparts. It wanted to designate a site in a rural area of Manitoba where there is very little industrial activity and high unemployment rates on which would be established a $60-million oriented strandboard plant. That plant would provide 130 direct jobs plus employment in gathering and hauling the wood to the site. Of course, government funding was required, but the bulk of the funding would come from the private sector. Again, there has been no response from the federal Government.
There was a proposal that the Red River Community College, the large community college established in the City of Winnipeg, have its learning resource centre expanded. The present facility which was built some years ago was built to accommodate about 2,700 students. It now services over 5,000 full-time and several thousand part-time students.
I do not have to remind Hon. Members of the tremendous revolutions that are taking place in computers and their use and the need to expand the software which services those computers. It seems to me that the community college proposal has merit which no one can dispute. It is the high technology areas where we will find the jobs we will need for young people entering the job market and for those who will be displaced as traditional manufacturing industries become more efficient or obsolete. That is the kind of project we need, and we need it now.
A series of reports have been written as a result of studies done in Ontario and articles appearing in various journals telling us how badly we are doing in training Canadians, both young Canadians who will enter the job market in the next year or two and adults who are finding their jobs have become
obsolete. We are not doing the job which is required. There was a report in The Globe and Mail either yesterday or today which said that many of our manufacturing industries which are moving into more highly sophisticated operations are telling us that we do not have the skilled workers required. We do not have the tool and die makers, the machinists or the people qualified in the newest electronics jobs. This proposal came from the Government of Manitoba that the community college be expanded and modernized so that it could do the job required. What did we hear from the federal Government? Nothing.
The people of Manitoba want to know why this situation is continuing. They want to know why these very practical proposals which have come from the Government of Manitoba have been ignored and downgraded by the federal Government.
One of the specific proposals made by the Government of Manitoba concerned increased procurement by the federal Government in the West. This is one area in which the Conservatives have consistently promised they will do better because this is something they consistently harped on when they were in opposition. I was here on many occasions when western Conservative Members and Atlantic Conservative Members complained loudly, and justifiably, that under the Liberal Government-

speakeroldname: Mr. John R. Rodriguez (Nickel Belt) moved
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CANADA PENSION PLAN MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
that Bill C-250, an Act to amend the Canada Pension Plan (survivor's pension), be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Madam Speaker, I should start off with the genesis of Bill C-250 which seeks to amend the Canada Pension Plan Act, Section 44(l)(d).
The reason I presented this Bill, and have been presenting it since 1979, and it is a very tragic reason, is because of a 40-year old miner who was killed in the mines in Sudbury. After the tragedy of burying the miner, his spouse, having to get on
March 14, 1988

with her life with her dependants, went to the local Canada Pension Plan office to apply for survivor's benefits for herself and her dependants under the Act. She filled out the form and the person dealing with her said he was sorry but she did not qualify for survivor's benefits. She asked why she did not qualify for survivor's benefits. He said she did not qualify because she was 34 years of age.
Under the Canada Pension Plan Act, Section 44(l)(d), any surviving spouse under the age of 35 is not eligible to collect survivor's benefits. Not a penny. Here we have a widow with two dependent children, who had not been in the workforce since she had been married, being told that she would get at that time about $80 a month for each of the children and she would have to go on welfare.
There is another example of an older gentleman who went to Poland. He met and fell in love with a young woman and brought her back to Canada. He was in his late 50s, she in her late 20s. They had one child before he dropped dead of a heart attack one day. She was ineligible to collect survivor's benefits under the Act. Again, the invocation of Section 44(1 )(d). What does that section say? It says:
a survivor's pension shall be paid to the surviving spouse, as determined pursuant to this Act, of a deceased contributor who has made contributions for not less than the minimum qualifying period if, the surviving spouse has
(i)	reached 65 years of age, or
(ii)	in the case of a surviving spouse who has not reached 65 years of age,
(A) had at the time of the death of the contributor reached 35 years of age.
She had not reached the age of 35 at the time of the death of her spouse and she would not be eligible for survivor's benefits. I would like to say unequivocally that that is discrimination based on age.
This issue was looked at by the parliamentary task force on pension reform chaired by the Hon. Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith). The task force, after considering a large number of proposals and briefs, concluded that before comprehensive changes to the Canada Pension Plan survivor's benefits could be recommended, further study was required. That further study was done. A White Paper was issued which looked at the Canada Pension Plan and specifically at the question of survivor's provisions. I just want to read from page 39 of that White Paper published in September, 1987, just last fall. It said:
Survivors who are under age 35 at the time of the death of their spouse, and who are not caring for a dependent child of the contributor, are not eligible for a survivor benefit until they reach age 65, unless they are disabled or become disabled.
We know that is what is provided for. This White Paper recognizes the discriminatory nature of Section 44(1 )(d) and recommends that the surviving spouse ought to get the Canada Pension Plan benefit irrespective of age.
The report of the parliamentary committee on equality rights, in 1985, on page 40, under the subtitle "Benefits for Surviving Spouses" had this to say:
Canada Pension Plan
Although CPP benefits for surviving spouses are not restricted to female spouses, it seems clear that these eligibility rules are based on assumptions about the dependency of women that may no longer be valid and that are unfair on their face. For example, the exclusion of spouses under 35 years of age who are neither disabled nor have dependent children is probably based on the theory that surviving spouses in their twenties and early thirties usually have little difficulty in finding employment or remarrying.
That committee recognized as well the discriminatory nature of Section 44(l)(d). It goes on to recommend that it be removed from the Act.
It seems to me that in that Act, when it deals with surviving spouses, there are other discriminatory provisions. If the surviving spouse is under 45 but over 35, they get a partial pension. They do not get the full pension. Their benefits are reduced by 1 1 /20th for each month he or she is under 45. This works out to a pension of roughly $145.18.
The age provisions are clearly discriminatory and are contrary to the Charter of Rights. In fact, this whole question of survivor's benefits under the Canada Pension Plan Act are under review by the parliamentary committee which is studying the White Paper on survivor benefits under the Canada Pension Plan. I would hope that the committee, too, will recognize the discriminatory nature of Section 44(1 )(d). In fact, I have been informed that both the provinces and the federal Government recognize that 44(1 )(d) is indeed discriminatory. Therefore, why do we have to wait?
Canada Pension Plan officials in my riding told a woman who was under 35 who appeared before them seeking survivor's benefits that they could not give her the benefit but that she should take the issue to the Human Rights Commission and appeal through the process. We all know that to go through the courts is a very costly and protracted route. I do not know where poor people would get the money to challenge Section 44(1 )(d) of the Canada Pension Plan Act. If what I have heard is true, that the federal Government, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), and his provincial counterparts have recognized the discriminatory nature of 44(l)(d), then surely with that kind of unanimity and with determination of purpose it would be easy to bring in an amendment to the Act.
I am sure that Members on this side of the House would be only too pleased to expedite an amendment to the Act which would create justice and remove an obviously discriminatory section of the Act. Incidentally, the reason I brought Bill C-250 forward was the very fact that we could expedite it and not have to put poor people through a whole process of legalisms which could go on indefinitely.
As an aside to the main purpose of this Bill, I have discovered that the federal Government has made certain changes to the benefits under the Canada Pension Plan disability benefits. These were all improvements to give recipients an increase in their pensions. However, private sector employers have been grabbing the money instead of allowing the

March 14, 1988
Canada Pension Plan
pensioners to get the increases. Even more outrageous, provincial Governments have been grabbing the increases which the federal Government has granted to those who are in receipt of disability pensions. The Province of Ontario is blatant in its grabbing from the pockets of the disabled and the poor. It is reducing the community and social services benefits to the poor. The Government of Ontario is reaching on to the table and taking the bread and meat right off the tables of poor people. I think that is a disgrace.
I have written to the Minister of National Health and Welfare about this, but all I hear back is that they are discussing it with the provinces. Well, that is not good enough. They have been discussing it with the provinces for two years and that is not good enough for the poor who have an entitlement to a disbility pension.
I ask Members not to let this Bill go the way of other Private Members' Bills which are debated for an hour and then talked out. I ask Members not to talk the Bill out, to take this opportunity to make a strike for what is right and just. For once, let this Bill go to committee, especially since the Government is in agreement that Section 44(l)(d) is indeed discriminatory.
I appeal to Members to let the Bill go. Do not talk the Bill out but let it go to committee so that we can eventually have the Act amended. I will not take credit for it. If the Government wants the credit for it, that is fine with me. I am prepared to erase C-250 from the front of the Bill and put the Minister's name there in lights. I am just a humble Member in this House. I do not seek the glory of having an amendment made to the Act. The Government can have the credit. All I want is justice for the poor people of the country who have been discriminated against, particularly women upon whom it has fallen harder than it has on men.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CANADA PENSION PLAN MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate and I would like to begin by saying to the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), whose Private Members' Bill we are discussing today, that while I might question his contention that he is just a humble Member of the House, because I think he is far more than whatever those words may imply, I do not in any way question his sincerity. I would applaud him for that and for his persistence in ensuring that this issue, which has been brought before the House on many occasions, remains before the House. In fact, I think he understands that the Government is as committed as is he to addressing the principles of the Bill before us.
As most Members know, the proposal set forth in Bill C-250 is an important and topical one. The issues of age discrimination and other equality considerations in the context of the Canada Pension Plan are an active concern of the Government at this time. In fact, on September 24, 1987, a consultation paper on survivor benefits under the Canada Pension Plan was tabled in the House of Commons and was referred to the
standing committee. We are still eagerly looking forward to the standing committee's report.
In other words, Madam Speaker, we are now in the process of a major review of Canada Pension Plan survivor provisions. This review was undertaken so that federal and provincial Governments, which share jurisdiction over the Canada Pension Plan, could determine the most appropriate way to bring the plan's survivor benefits directly in line with equality provisions under the new Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and in line with changes in family structure and other social changes that have taken place in Canada since the CPP's inception some 22 years ago.
When the Canada Pension Plan was being designed in the early 1960s the majority of Canadian families were one-earner families. Legislators therefore decided that when a contributor died a portion of his or her Canada Pension Plan retirement pension would be paid to the surviving spouse in certain circumstances. The benefit levels and eligibility requirements for survivor pensions were based on specific criteria which reflected the then current assumption that the majority of married women were financially dependent on their spouse for life. These dependency criteria included the recipient's age, the presence of dependent children or a disability, and a survivor's eligibility for other benefits under the plan.
During the pension reform discussions of recent years numerous Canadians have indicated that they share the Hon. Member's dissatisfaction with the Canada Pension Plan's existing structure for survivor benefits. Many have suggested that the dependency criterion has become outmoded and arbitrary and may be discriminatory in light of the Charter. There has been a growing perception, moreover, that application of the current survivor benefit eligibility criteria have resulted too often in a level of income protection inconsistent with the situation of Canadians who have become widowed.
As Hon. Members are aware, major changes to the Canada Pension Plan do require the approval of two-thirds of the Canadian provinces having two-thirds of the Canadian population, as well as the approval of Parliament. Federal and provincial legislators did reach a consensus on a comprehensive restructuring of Canada Pension Plan survivor benefits in time for such a reform to be included in Bill C-l 16.
Nevertheless, a federal-provincial working group of officials was established expressly for the purpose of re-examining the role of CPP survivor provisions in light of equality provisions under the Charter, as well as in view of growing pressure to improve benefit adequacy and the over-all context of social changes. In pursuing this task, the working group reviewed the substantial body of recommendations and other input which had already been presented to legislators and which has remained a matter of official record. The consultation paper on CPP survivor benefits, which presents a comprehensive
March 14, 1988

proposal for reform, and to which I and my hon. friend made reference earlier, was developed as a direct result of this study.
In essence, the proposals outlined in the consultation paper have provided us with a sound but flexible basis for public discussion and the means for determining whether the requisite consensus for a major reform of CPP survivor provisions exists or, alternatively, can be arrived at among both legislators and the public at large.
The consultation paper proposes a new benefit structure for future survivors that responds to the equality provisions under the Charter and to projected social changes. It also proposes improvements to the existing CPP structure to ensure that current survivors would also be treated in accordance with the Charter.
Finally, it proposes increases in benefits payable on behalf of children. Eligibility for CPP survivor benefits under the new structure, therefore, would not be based directly on considerations of age, disability and family status, as was the case during the first two decades of this plan's existence.
The consultation paper's proposals recognize instead, that financial difficulties may be experienced by surviving spouses of all ages, and that such difficulties may be greater and longer lasting when young children are present. The paper recognizes that a Canadian family's subsistence today is increasingly based on the gainful employment of both spouses and on the pension protection accumulated by each.
Reflecting these circumstances, the paper proposes to pay substantially higher monthly benefits concentrated over the difficult years of adjustment following a spouse's death, normally five years, rather than much lower lifetime payments. If implemented, this proposed new structure would initially apply only to future generations of younger Canadians as they experience widowhood. In recognition that all widowed individuals face a degree of difficulty following bereavement, the proposed new structure would provide surviving spouses with benefits on an equal basis, in accordance with the deceased spouse's CPP record of earnings.
Survivors who are carrying for dependent children would, however, be eligible for benefits over a longer period. As well, the consultation paper proposes important increases for CPP benefits payable in respect of dependent children of a deceased CPP contributor.
As I have stated, the consultation paper also proposes that benefits under the existing structure be substantially modified. Such changes would apply to current beneficiaries, as well as to the current older generation of Canadians who, in the event of being widowed at a future date, would have the option of choosing coverage under either the improved existing structure or the proposed new benefit structure.
Improvements to the current structure would include doubling the flat rate portion of CPP survivor benefits payable to all survivors under age 65. As well, the reductions which currently apply to survivors younger than age 45 would be
Canada Pension Plan
eliminated, and survivors who, to date, have been denied CPP survivor payments because they were younger than age 35 when their spouse died-the Hon. Member referred to such a tragic case-would become eligible to receive benefits under the plan. Finally, children's benefits would have the same improvements that would be implemented under the proposed new benefit structure.
With regard to Bill C-250, the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt hopefully will be assured that Canadians are already in full agreement with his sentiments.
At the same time, it is important to recognize that federal and provincial legislators should not and cannot amend the CPP in haste. As I have explained, major amendments to the plan require a high level of consensus among the Canadian public and among legislators at both levels.
The federal Government, nevertheless, is committed to making changes as soon as such a consensus can be achieved. We may expect, therefore, to proceed with further consultation and negotiation among concerned Canadians, as soon as the Government has received the report of the Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CANADA PENSION PLAN MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate on Bill C-250. When examining the premise upon which the legislation is being suggested by the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), I find that the basic intent of the Bill is to eliminate discrimination from the current provisions of the Canada Pension Plan in relation to widow's benefits or survivor's benefits. The notion of eliminating discrimination on the basis of age is a laudable one theoretically. However, one can see that even in the context of the Bill itself, it still has an unequal application. To my knowledge, the effect of passing his amendment would be to say that any person who is a survivor would be entitled to a benefit. Presumably, that person would be entitled to a benefit until the age 65 when a different benefit package would kick in. Quite clearly, even with that cut-off point, there is discrimination on the basis of age.
While eliminating discrimination on the basis of age may sound good in principle, there may be practical reasons to have discrimination on the basis of age.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CANADA PENSION PLAN MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
They would switch to regular CPP at age
65.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CANADA PENSION PLAN MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
I understand that they would switch to regular CPP at 65, but I am simply saying that the principle of eliminating age discrimination sounds good in theory but may not always be applicable in practice.
Let me point out one area where I believe the principle of this Bill would not stand up to serious examination. It is an area within some of the discussion paper that relates to survivors' benefits and about which we were extremely concerned in the standing committee.

March 14, 1988
Canada Pension Plan
Let us consider the situation of a widow over the age 45. The discussion paper is based on the theory that as more and more women enter the workforce, since women tend to be the recipient in the application of spouse's benefits, the Government felt it might be better to provide them with a short-term bridging benefit of a period of three years' additional help. They would be expected to reintegrate into the workforce following this, and earn money that would then eliminate the necessity for survivor's benefits.
Statistics show that more and more young women are entering the workforce whether or not they have children, school age and below. I believe the flaw in the Member's Bill relates to the discussion of survivors between the ages of 45 and 65. The discussion paper suggests that since women are entering the workforce in greater numbers, they should be allowed this bridging benefit and be able to go into the workforce after this three-year period to compete essentially for the same wage as their male counterpart.
Two factors were discussed in the context of our response to the discussion paper which have not been touched on today. These factors, I believe, are relevant in the context of awarding survivors' benefits. First is the question of earnings. If we look at the typical woman under the age of 45, currently widowed, we find that 74.4 per cent actually reported earnings in 1985. We do not specify exactly at what amount those earnings are placed, but basically three-quarters of the widowed population at that point would be earning some kind of salary outside the home. That number drops, when one looks at widowed women between the ages of 45 and 54 years, to 67.2 per cent. Subsequent to that we see a dramatic drop in the number of widowed women between the ages of 55 and 64 years reporting earnings, so much so that only 38.7 per cent actually reported any earnings in 1985. That means that as public policy makers we may want to examine a policy in relation to survivor's benefits which is in fact discriminatory in a positive sense towards those older women who may not have a significant chance of re-entering the workforce.
Another element which we felt would certainly be relevant in the context of determining Canada Pension Plan benefits is again related to age statistics. It is the question of how many widowed women will go on to remarry and into a second financial partnership. For those people who are widowed under the age of 35 years, according to figures based on 1984 statistics, we can expect that 77.6 per cent of those particular widows will go on to remarry. However, if we look at the age category of 45 to 54 years, we find that only 38.9 per cent of that particular group can be expected to remarry. Obviously, if they are not entering into a second legal and financial partnership, their needs will be quite different. Again, those needs may be quantifiably different on the basis of age.
If we look at the category of widowed women between the ages of 55 and 64 years, we find that only 28.8 per cent will be going on to a second marriage. Therefore, the vast majority of
widowed women over the age of 45 years do not expect to enter into another legal partnership of marriage or a financial partnership. So they will be totally on their own.
I do not feel it is realistic for us as public policy makers to say that in practical application there should not necessarily be discrimination on the basis of age. In fact, I think the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt was one of those who has been highly critical of the Government for not responding specifically with its promise to the older workers in the form of a replacement for the Labour Adjustments Benefits program.
The Labour Adjustment Benefits Program was a policy of the previous Liberal Government to provide long-term assistance to workers over the age of 55 years, in the so-called "sunset" category of industries. Those workers were eligible on the basis of their age. As public policy makers we recognize the principle that at a certain age and stage of one's life, one's chances of re-employment are much diminished. That is why I think that while the principle on the surface looks laudable, in practice, if we apply the principle that there should be absolutely no discrimination on the basis of age in the area of Canada Pension Plan benefits, we may cut off our nose to spite our face in the sense that we will not be able to help older widows who will, of necessity, need our help the most.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CANADA PENSION PLAN MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first of all I would like to thank the Hon. Member, whose talents are also much appreciated on the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, for his insights and his interest in improving the survivor's benefits program under the Canada Pension Plan. I also wish to thank him for giving us this opportunity to consider a matter that, I believe, encompasses far more than merely eliminating the age factor from the present framework of survivor's benefits. I am of course referring to the possibility of the surviving spouse being under 65.
Madam Speaker, I think that in addition to the age factor, we should also be examining the basis of the entire structure of survivor's benefits as it now exists. I do not want to give the impression, however, that I disagree with the structure established by the fathers of the Canada Pension Plan when the Plan was set up in the sixties. This Plan was designed to respond to the needs of the sixties, and we can say that all things considered, it has worked quite well, thank you!
It is a fact, however, that the premises on which the present structure of survivor's benefits is based are no longer as relevant today and in fact have almost lost their raison d'etre.
The society in which we live today no longer corresponds to the projection made of that society in the sixties or even to the image extrapolated at the time.
The social conditions that prevailed during that period have changed-some will say for the worse, others for the better-
March 14, 1988

and meanwhile, the structure of the survivor's benefits program has remained virtually the same, immutably laid down in the regulatory framework common to all Acts of Parliament.
The House will recall that the present structure of the survivor's benefits program under the Canada Pension Plan was designed mainly to guarantee income stability for surviving wives. This concept corresponded to the family situation prevailing when the Canada Pension Plan became effective in the sixties.
At the time, and we have to go back about 25 years, it was reasonable to expect that the contributions made by spouses to the family unit were well defined according to sex and reflected the traditional view that the wife was a mother and housewife, while the husband was the bread winner or wage earner. It was also reasonable to expect that the marriage would be long-lasting. Since women had little or no contact with the labour market for many years, it was expected that many women, especially if they were not old enough at the time of the decease of their spouse, would not be able to earn enough money to maintain their previous standard of living or be able to remarry or even to get by without necessarily maintaining their previous standard of living.
Madam Speaker, 20 years later, the same concept is still being used to provide the same kind of guarantees for persons who survive their spouses, although the situation has changed completely and is totally different from the conditions that prevailed 20 years ago. During the past two decades some major changes have taken place in the structure of the family unit and the role of spouses in that unit and in the economy. A striking example of it is the substantial increase in the number of women in the labour force.
Madam Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to name some of the most important changes that have taken place when women started achieving greater financial independence, and I will also provide some figures to illustrate those changes.
I suggest that my facts can be easily checked by referring directly to the various documents I consulted, and I intend to table a list of those documents later on.
Madam Speaker, I was saying that during the last couple of decades, the labour force participation rate of women had substantially increased. In fact, it has increased steadily since the fifties, and it is expected that by the year 2000, one out of every two workers will be a woman, although in 1950 the ratio was only one out of five. In other words, by the year 2000 the ratio will be the same in the labour force and the general population.
Considering, however, that women's labour force participation rate only reflects the number of working women as a percentage of the total labour force, we must be careful when using these figures because they also depend on the number of men in the labour force. For instance, if the number of men in
Canada Pension Plan
the labour force were to go down, this would raise the percentage of women in the labour force while there would be no increase in the actual number of working women.
Madam Speaker, that is why I think it is far more useful to consider the women's participation rate, which gives us the ratio of working women to the group of women 15 years or over. Between 1967 and 1985, which means from the time the regulations came into effect up to the present decade, the women's participation rate jumped from 40 per cent to about 70 per cent. We also see that the increase is largely due to the behaviour of married women, whose participation rate rose from 40 per cent in 1967 to 66 per cent in 1985, an increase of two-thirds. Various factors contributed to this increase.
1 think it is important to consider this development, because each of these more or less irreversible factors shows that the survivor's circumstances no longer are, and no longer will be, the same as they were during the past 20 or 30 years.
First of all, we have seen a change in women's attitudes to their traditional role and in the perception they have of themselves. Women no longer see marriage as the ultimate goal nor as a protective shield that will save them forever more from solitude and financial insecurity. The rising divorce rate observed in recent years is certainly a reflection of this change in attitude.
Madam Speaker, between 1970 and 1983-within a period of 13, not 25 years the divorce rate doubled. Women feel a need to become more self-reliant and provide for their own financial security. They have become aware of their own potential, shed the traditional and discriminatory stereotypes, get a better education in a wider variety of subjects and increasingly take charge of their own economic circumstances.
To a certain extent, we can measure these changes using a number of indicators. The marriage rate is dropping and the birth rate as well. We are also seeing people postponing marriage and the birth of their first child until they are older. Women are less likely to leave their jobs when they marry or when they have children.
If we look at the participation rate of women in terms of family situation and in terms of the presence of children, we see that even with preschool children, married women have doubled their participation rate. From 34 per cent in 1967, the participation rate of married women with children of preschool age went up to twice that rate, 68 per cent, in 1985. Women with school age children went from 40 per cent up to 70 per cent in 1985, an increase of 75 per cent over the rate observed 20 years before.
Madam Speaker, we can even conclude that although the presence of children tends to restrict women's participation in the labour force, it is less restrictive in 1981 than it was in 1971. We can also assume that on the whole, women are more likely to see their labour market participation as a permanent

March 14, 1988
Canada Pension Plan
activity, even if about 50 per cent of married women work part-time.
Madam Speaker, women's education has also changed dramatically in recent years. These changes are particularly noticeable at the university and college levels, where the number of women enrolled has increased considerably. Interestingly, women students at universities and colleges are majoring in a wider variety of subjects than was previously the case. They have made considerable inroads in fields that traditionally have been a male preserve, which to a certain extent is an indication of a definite change in orientation.
Madam Speaker, it also reflects a turning away from the kind of training that prepared for responsibilities within the home. They now tend the focus on careers that will keep them on the labour market.
Madam Speaker, I see you are signalling that my time is almost up. The Government is now waiting for the Standing Committee of the House on National Health and Welfare, which was asked to proceed with public hearings on the subject, to submit its report. In the light of the results of this major consultation process, this Government, after obtaining the approval of the provinces, will implement new measures to provide Canadian men and women, through the Canada Pension Plan, with a survivor's benefits program that is better adapted to their changing needs.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CANADA PENSION PLAN MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wish to congratulate the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) for giving us the opportunity to talk about this extremely important matter in the House today. He tells us he has been fighting this issue since 1979. I can only say that perhaps his arguments as presented over the years were what convinced and persuaded the federal Government and the provincial Governments to agree to bring about amendments to the Canada Pension Plan to do what the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt has been arguing about over the years.
While I welcome some of the improvements that are proposed in the discussion paper on survivor benefits I want to say that in my view some of the assumptions made in it are faulty. I have argued this in the Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare which is now seized of that document.
That document makes a number of assumptions which do not hold up. The first is that because there is a greater participation of women in the workforce there is less need to pay survivor benefits to those women. It neglects the fact that many of the jobs that have been created for women over the years are really part-time jobs. It does not address the need for adequate child care to allow women to re-enter the workforce. There are a number of problems in the discussion paper.
However, since the matter is before the Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare and since that committee is in the process of bringing a response forward to the discussion
paper I do not feel that I am at liberty to talk about the actual proposals that we are discussing. I see that the chairman of the committee, the Hon. Member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday) is sitting in the House today. I think it is safe enough to say without relating any confidences that that is one area of the discussion paper that would have received the unanimous support of the members of the committee. That is what I would have said 10 minutes ago, but since I heard the remarks of the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) on the Bill before the House I am not so sure whether or not it will be unanimous.
Quite frankly, I was surprised to hear the Hon. Member for Hamilton East make the type of criticisms against Bill C-250 that she made. What she seemed to argue is that discrimination against a woman under the age of 35 is okay because we need existing dollars under the Canada Pension Plan to go toward improvements for only women in higher age brackets. I see that the Hon. Member is shaking her head in a negative fashion. She seems to be saying that that is not what she meant.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CANADA PENSION PLAN MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: That is not what I said.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CANADA PENSION PLAN MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
What I thought the Hon. Member said was that only a certain amount of dollars is available dollars which exist in the Canada Pension Plan with which improvements can be made. She seemed to argue that with those available dollars we should be seriously directing those moneys towards improving benefits for those who are in the higher age brackets. That is what I thought she said.
However, the Hon. Member is now saying that that is not what she said. I am delighted to hear that. I have received correspondence from young women under the age of 35 who have been widowed. Many of these women are facing heavy financial responsibilities, especially where children are involved. First, there is the traumatic experience that they go through when their spouse dies, more often than not in a tragic way. They are then faced with the responsibility of bringing their children up without any kind of financial support in some cases, especially if they are not actively participating in the workforce at that time. This can make their lives extremely difficult.
The White Paper argues that if those amendments were not made to the Canada Pension Plan, it could be construed as being a violation of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms against younger women at age 35. I am hopeful that when the item is discussed in committee we will end up with a unanimous recommendation to put an end to this discrimination and to do the right thing by these younger people.
There are some other problems in the Canada Pension Plan which could have been addressed in the discussion paper but unfortunately were not. For example, many delays are being encountered between the time an individual lodges an appeal against a decision rendered by the pension board, the time the
March 14, 1988

appeal has been filed, and the time that it is heard. Very often it takes in excess of 12 months.
When the Minister proposed amendments to the Canada Pension Plan in 1986-and they were passed in the House in July of the same year, roughly about six weeks after they were proposed and introduced-he assured us that a new appeal process would be set up very quickly.
Last week I had occasion to ask the Minister why appeals were still taking in excess of 12 months, very often 18 months between the time when the individual files an appeal and the time the appeal is heard. That is absolutely ridiculous. What did the Minister say when I asked him that question in the House? He said that the problem was that they had to be careful because they did not want to get caught up in workmen's compensation cases and so on.
It was an entirely different answer from the one that the Minister gave to Ms. Alexa McDonough, the leader of the New Democratic Party in Nova Scotia, when he wrote to her on December 10, 1987. He said that while he recognized the delays in appeals, he would also recognize that the new appeal process had not even been set up yet.
There has been a passage of time of some 18 months since the House passed the legislation and the amendments which gave the Minister authority to establish a new appeal tribunal, and it still has not been set up. People who are suffering real financial hardship because of some disability and who very often have no other income except what they could receive under the Canada Pension Plan cannot get at it, because the Minister has not set up the proper appeal procedure which he assured us would speed up the appeal process.
It is time the Government got on with these kinds of things. Today we could approve the Bill which the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt has placed before the House. We could handle that one area very quickly without awaiting the report of the Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare, which would support this measure in any event. The Minister supports it. Why do we not go ahead with it rather than wait for months until the Department produces legislation? We should proceed with this piece of legislation today and do the right thing for those women under age 35 who are being discriminated against. Even the Minister recognizes that. Let us get on with it and remove the discrimination once and for all.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CANADA PENSION PLAN MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to begin by congratulating the Hon. Member who introduced the Bill. He did not have the wisdom to choose the right political Party, but he had the wisdom to choose parents who live in the riding of Scarborough West whom I am honoured to represent. I also congratulate him for being a good example of the opportunities afforded any Member of Parliament to initiate legislative debate and creative discussion as he has done with this Bill. I have known him to do it with others, such as the Bill on lobbying when it
Canada Pension Plan
was my honour and pleasure to sit with him on the committee responsible for that legislation.
Again we see an example of a Member introducing a legislative proposal as far back as 1979 and reintroducing it as recently as this afternoon. I confidently believe that that seed sown and developed is about to come to fruition. He has made the suggestion that the Private Member's Bill number might be taken off and the Minister might reintroduce it as his recommendation. That gracious suggestion is one which I think may well prove to be the result of the debate this afternoon.
We will see the proposal contained in the Bill strengthened by the report and recommendations of the Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare, with further consideration by the Government itself. We will bring back to the House proposals which will meet not only the needs of the people referred to this afternoon but will provide assistance for more Canadians facing difficulty and challenge in this day. As a result of this legislative and governmental process, we will probably see a much better program or better legislative proposal than we might embrace today, even as good as it is.
I would hope that all Hon. Members of the House would see the necessity for the kind of review which is approaching a conclusion that we trust will be a happy one. One reason is the enormity of the size of the program to which we are referring. The survivor's pension program is in itself of incredible and impressive size. Some 483,000 spouses are receiving benefits as a result of the program, as are 94,000 orphans, at a cost to the public of 51,245 million. This manifests the kind of effort which the country is ready to put forward as we endeavour through such programs to assist each other.
We are seeing a need for careful review of the program so that we provide as much assistance to those who need it as is possible for a Government to do, as is possible for a public to do. That is what we are aiming to do. The very size of the program in terms of the figures I have cited shows the need for the process in which we are now involved and will carry it to its happy conclusion.
We must be sure that when the Bill receives the benefit of major amendments-and they will be major-that we have presented to us by the Government a Bill which comprehends the social change that has been a feature of the country's development since the Canada Pension Plan was first initiated. Certainly the number of working spouses is much larger today, and it is but one example of the way in which the social environment has been profoundly altered. Therefore, the kind of program we as a Government will wish to introduce will be one which comprehends all dimensions.
It is vital that all Members of the House and all members of the public concerned about this matter, including the large number watching the debate, be aware that it is not possible for this House or this Parliament on its own to provide the kind of change we want to provide for people who need it most. We have a complex method for amending Canada Pension

March 14, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
Plan legislation. It requires full consultation with the provinces, including the approval and support of two-thirds of the provincial Governments representing two-thirds of the population of Canada. It is necessary for us to carry forward the process which I have described, not only in terms of the committee and the Elouse, but also in terms of further consultation with the provinces.
Therefore, I welcome the Bill which has been presented to us this afternoon. I see it in terms of a seed that will lead to full development and the fruition of a legislative proposal by the Government which will adequately meet the need in this regard.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, during the speech by one of the Conservative Members from Manitoba, he asked why the New Democratic Party would be opposed to free trade with the United States when Manitoba Hydro was receiving billions of dollars in the export of its energy to the United States. Would the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) answer the question: Why would the NDP be opposed to something which the Conservative Member from Manitoba said was such a good thing?

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the one point made by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Minaker) with which I could agree is that Manitoba Hydro has been successful in completing contracts for sales of hydroelectric power to the midwest United States of about $3.5 billion, and more to come.
The reason the Manitoba Government opposed the so-called free trade agreement is that it does not protect future sales against opposition, which could well be successful, by American interests. There is nothing in the agreement as it is drafted at the present time which would prevent the coal producers in the United States from claiming that hydroelectric power from Manitoba or Quebec or British Columbia is subsidized. For example, in the Manitoba situation the federal Government helped finance the transmission lines which carry the power from northern Manitoba to Winnipeg and then farther to the United States. There is nothing to prevent coal companies or oil companies, if oil is again in surplus supply, or natural gas companies from bringing anti-dumping charges against us and calling for countervail duties to be imposed on the sale of power.
In the agreement, the definition regarding electricity has been changed. Electricity has gone from being an intangible, which it was up until now, to being classified as goods. That will make it easier for the people and interests in the United States who want to stop the sale and export of power from Manitoba or from any of the other provinces and it will make it easier for the Americans to invoke their anti-dumping claims.
There is something else which should be of interest to the people of Saskatchewan and Ontario. Under the terms of this agreement, it would be within the ability of the provincial hydroelectric utility, whether Manitoba, British Columbia or Quebec, to sell power to neighboring provinces. In the case of Manitoba, it is to sell power to Saskatchewan or Ontario at a price lower than it could sell power to the United States. That is very important. We take the view, and I think most Canadians take the view, that the resources of Canada may, under our constitution, be the responsibility of the individual provinces, but they certainly would hope and expect that the resources would be used to the advantage of all people. To say that the Americans can buy power at the same price as we might want to sell power to another province seems to be something we ought to oppose.
Lastly, Manitoba, like other provinces, has been looking at the possibility of establishing an aluminum processing plant in Manitoba. We have huge amounts of potential power to be developed. This agreement with the United States disallows incentive arrangements to be made for energy intensive industries. We cannot give a special deal or a cheaper price to an aluminum company or any other energy intensive using industry at a price that we would not permit the Americans. For all these reasons and others, the Manitoba Government has opposed the free trade agreement.
March 14, 1988

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture

What surprises me is the suggestion by the Hon. Member, if I understood him correctly, that the Manitoba Government may be guilty, to use his words, of dumping hydroelectricity in the United States. He seems to be signalling that to the United States. Does the Hon. Member believe that the Manitoba Government is dumping electricity in the United States and that it would be subject to countervail?

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext:
No, Madam Speaker, of course I do not believe that. It has not happened. The Manitoba Government sells surplus power from the new generating plants. If Manitoba can complete the negotiations, it proposes to develop another power plant which will produce a great deal of power and it will sell a substantial part of that power to the United States. Of course it is not subsidized except in some of the ways which I have mentioned.
Talking about countervail, I wish the Hon. Member would give some thought to the views expressed, not publicly yet or very often, but certainly expressed privately by many leaders of farm organizations. They are worried that despite this agreement, the American and farm interests will be able to apply countervail duties against farm products being exported to the United States whenever they feel markets are being challenged. I wish the Hon. Member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Clark), who represents so many farmers, would give some thought to that kind of problem.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on western diversification. Having listened to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) on the subject of hydroelectricity, surely he does not expect me to believe that the Province of Manitoba has undertaken the massive hydroelectric projects it has undertaken without first having some pretty firm commitments of markets to the south of the 49th parallel. If that be the case, then in my view that would just add one more very valid reason why the NDP will probably be rejected in the next provincial election.
I would also like to comment on the absence of an understanding of the difference between consumer-oriented power and power for commercial reasons. Perhaps if the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North were to review the trade agreement, he would gain enlightenment on the subject.
I would like to speak on behalf of the proponents of the very innovative, very timely western diversification program. One of
Western Economic Diversification Act
the main features of this program is the fact that it will frequently accept under its terms of reference projects which would otherwise fall through the cracks. It will accept projects that do not quite meet the requirements of the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, programs that do not quite fit the Department of Science and Technology or the subagreement in forestry or tourism with the Province of British Columbia or with any other province. The fact is that under western diversification, there will be an opportunity to assist that did not prevail before.
It is in that context that I wish to talk about the rather unique circumstance of a body of fresh water which is the longest navigable freshwater body in western North America.
I am speaking of a stretch of water on the Columbia River from the Grand Coulee Dam in south central Washington State to Revelstoke, British Columbia, on the Trans-Canada Highway, a distance of some 350 miles.
The U.S. side of this body of water is now being enjoyed and will, I hope, be further enjoyed by the marine tourism sector. The American side has been totally surveyed for hydrographic charting, but the minute we hit the Canada-U.S. border, we discover that there is a blank space on the map. There is an outline of a lake and the towns and communities are identified, but there is no navigational chart available.
In order to prepare a navigational chart which would extend from the Canada-U.S. border to Revelstoke, one would be looking at an expenditure of about half a million dollars. It would be a very detailed study involving aerial photography and the depth of the lake measured in increments over a distance of a few metres, back and forth across the lake. It would take about five months. Then all that information would have to be correlated into charts. This is complicated by the fact that from Castlegar north, we are dealing with a body of water which is subject to substantial fluctuation by virtue of the Columbia River Treaty and the storage dams on that river.
That project really does not fit any other mould, but I am hopeful that under western diversification, we will see that project funded early. It may be that the Department of Fisheries and Oceans could be the provider of assistance. However, it also happens to have priorities of a navigational nature in the Beaufort Sea where we are continuing to look for new oil and gas discoveries. The Department has some emergency work to do in the Hecate Strait off northern Vancouver Island, so in order to get this project going, we find that there is a possibility that it will fit the western diversification fund.
There is another project going on in Kootenay West. A company called Kootenay Tractor will hopefully be in a position to purchase an entire product line from the United States to manufacture a log-forwarder. One might say that that is fine, we are glad to see a company from the United States go into production in Canada, but where is the diversification there. The diversification lies in the fact that the dealer of this particular log-forwarder has, on the basis of his own

March 14, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
experience, upgraded and strengthened the equipment so that it will be a more valuable and practical asset in the steep-slope terrain of British Columbia. Again, I hope that this project will fit the western diversification fund.
When we are talking about western diversification, we must also look at other areas where assistance under the western diversification fund is possible. Forentek is a major research facility for the forest industry, paid for largely by industry but in part by Government. Feric is a like institute of research. One institute is researching the end products and by-products of the forest industry and one is researching the need for value-added forest products. After all, about 50 per cent of all wood we export from Canada into the United States is value added in the United States. Clearly, by improving our capacity to diversify by value adding, we are creating new opportunities for employment and we are creating new products for the world. That opportunity exists within the research facilities of these institutes on the UBC campus.
Much of the equipment and machinery used, including computerized turnkey sawmills, comes from Germany and some of it comes from Sweden. There was a recent conference in Edmonton which I had the privilege of attending with the Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Merrithew) and his Parliamentary Secretary. Canada's industry is now determined to move to a number one position in value-added commodities in the forest sector and in the production of world-class forestry equipment. That determination was made clear at that three-day conference.
Forentek and Feric are the kinds of institutes that will help us get an additional leg-up through western diversification, thus creating more and more jobs. That is the bottom line.
I must return to the concept that is so often touted by our socialist friends. They say that we have a Government which persists in keeping the people of the West drawers of water, hewers of wood and pumpers of oil and gas, and there is no diversification. Yet when we provide the opportunity for diversification, they decry it. They say things that are most uncomplimentary. There is an absence of fact and an absence of understanding.
I believe that this stems from the mind-set of the socialist. Socialists would rather wallow in misery than see success. I cannot understand why they cannot enjoy success and share the enjoyment, pride and pleasure of success. No, they would rather say that the people of British Columbia are still hewers of wood and drawers of water. That is where our Party philosophies are at opposite ends of the spectrum.
I sometimes think that socialists were weaned on pickles. I see the attitude of NDP Members in their voting record. They voted against the repeal of the National Energy Program. That certainly tells me that they supported it at its outset.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext: So did the Conservatives.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext:
My colleague shouting from across the floor has not been seized by the facts.
The NDP marched lock-step down the road with Marc Lalonde on the National Energy Program. They voted against its repeal, knowing full well the economic disaster it had created in Saskatchewan, northern British Columbia, Alberta and even in the southern part of Manitoba. They also voted against the PGRT. They did not want to see the western energy accord succeed. They did not want to see the petroleum and natural gas industry take off. Why would they? That is success, and that is not cast in the mould of the NDP. They hate success. They want to be able to wallow in misery. Thank heaven that so many of us share a different attitude.
I have to support the comments of my colleague from Edmonton South who spoke so eloquently on this issue. However, having listened to the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) and his comments on agriculture and what this Conservative Government failed to do, we should look at the socialist record. The NDP voted against a $500,000 capital gains exemption for farmers. They did not want the farmer to smell success or have some measure of financial security after a lifetime of labour on and investment in his own land. The NDP voted against the expenditure of $92 million for drought relief for western farmers. Farmers on the Prairies will be reminded of that not just in the next federal election but in the ensuing weeks in Manitoba.
The NDP voted against providing the Canadian Wheat Board with $200 million to meet its deficit. Why? Where is the support they espouse for the prairie farmer? Did they vote against these measures because they wanted farmers to have more? Or, did they vote against them because they did not understand the purpose of the motion? Or, did they vote against them just on the principle that they could not possibly bring themselves to support the Government in power?
Their rhetoric is the rhetoric of failure, failure to recognize success. If that be their particular bag, then I say let them carry on with it. However, I have no hesitation, when I look at the western diversification program, in saying how fine it is that the essential requirement which will determine the acceptability of proposals will be the contribution each project or activity makes to the diversification of the western economy. What better aim or ambition could there be?
What about Kootenay West? How do I feel when I see the forest industry in a slump? They all have that slump. It is very much a creature of the market-place. How do I feel when the price of metals drops off the scale and miners are out of work? How do I feel when Cominco cuts back on its employees as it did in the massive lay-offs we experienced in my constituency in 1985 and 1986? No other alternative to turn to. There has been no diversification, but now it is starting to happen. It started even before this program came into being. It started with the support of this Government and my personal support.
March 14, 1988

We are seeing some examples of diversification which will help to take those students fresh out of high school or college and give them new skills in new technologies which will provide for them in the future.
Where is the future in tying the prairie provinces inextricably to agriculture? Where is the future in tying Alberta to the petroleum industry, or cattle, without adding value to the product? Where is the future? This Government had the foresight to address that issue because it came to office with one fundamental commitment to Canada: jobs, jobs, jobs. While the unemployment numbers in Kootenay West are far from satisfying to me, at least 1 know they are nowhere near the point they were in 1984. At least I know that western diversification is going to work for my constituency and is working, just as Community Futures is working, just as other programs of the Government of Canada are working.
When it comes to expenditures and federal involvement in Kootenay West from September of 1984 until today, I will stack our record against anything accomplished by any other Member over the last 30 years.
I have no hesitation in supporting this program. I am proud of the Government for introducing it. It is a match for the Atlantic Accord and will help generate new technologies and new kinds of employment opportunities for young Canadians. With that I thank you for the opportunity to address the Elouse this evening.
