speechtext: Questions or comments.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member referred to the downturn in the oil and gas industry in western Canada, cut-backs in exploration and everything else that happened. He described that situation in the early 1980s as being caused by the National Energy Program. What he did not say is that in the U.S., which did not have an NEP but which did have the most pro-business President it has had in the last 50 years, Exxon, which invested $4 billion in developing a plant to extract oil from shale in Colorado, shut down that plant because the price of oil had dropped so far.
The world price of oil right now is below $15 U.S. a barrel. That means exploration and development by the major companies is going to be cut back because there is a surplus for the foreseeable future. If that happens in Canada, as has already happened in the U.S., who will the Member and his Conservative Party blame for it since they did away with the NEP?

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for using that as an example. I cannot think of a more unfortunate example than oil extraction from shale. It is probably the most costly undertaking one could conceivably make in the oil and gas industry. I have to say that the extraction of that analogy from the precincts of the Hon. Member's thoughts is really begging the question and stretching credibility.
Western Economic Diversification Act
He talks about the difference between Canada and the U.S. and says that the NEP really was not that harmful. If his memory serves him well he will perhaps remember, or perhaps he has been told, that when the NEP was introduced, literally hundreds and hundreds of trucks containing oil rigs-and the Hon. Member might tell me if he knows approximately how many flatbeds it takes to move one standard rig-were lined up at the border as they headed south. An entire exploration industry moved out of the Province of Alberta and into the United States to get into the oil and gas discovery process. That was because of the National Energy Program.
I was in Alberta at the time that this was happening. I watched all the little service sectors which are so important to the industry fold. I saw small towns in which the economic base was the oil and gas service industry where one in ten houses was for sale. Twenty-two trucks of Canadian FracMas-ter in Red Deer for fracing in the oil sector sat idle, every one of them with $.5 million in high technology sitting on them. Only five were operating. People do drop things down drill holes, hence the need for tool retrieval companies, which were also idle. Commercial or industrial laundries which handled the oil-ridden clothes and cloths from the worksite were idle, jobs were gone.
I went into Fort St. John during that period and you could fire a cannon down the main street without hitting anything. Yet, before the National Energy Program was introduced you could not get a hotel room in Fort St. John to save your soul unless you had a reservation two weeks in advance. It was on that basis that one company of which I am aware decided that it would respond to that need in Fort St. John and build a hotel. It got built, and it went broke. It was a very unfortunate opening because it opened at about the time that Marc Lalonde, with his colleagues from the NDP, brought in the National Energy Program.
There is only one person whom I know in Alberta, whose name is known to Canadians, who has the courage today to stand up and say: "I supported the National Energy Program". I am darned if I know how he has avoided the lynch mob. That is Mel Hurtig. There is a man who really pushes his credibility and his luck. In spite of everything, he has been the beneficiary of a couple of million dollars from this Government for his excellent works on The Canadian Encyclopedia.
The fact is that Mr. Hurtig supported the National Energy Program in spite of the fact that he was well aware of the economic and social disaster which it created in the Province of Alberta, in northern British Columbia, in southern Saskatchewan, and even in the heavy oil of southern Manitoba.
If the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North wants to wax eloquent and use as an argument the fact that Exxon stopped work on oil extraction from shale on the basis of the oil price of $14, $15, $18, or $20 a barrel, that is not a very good basis for an argument.

March 14, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak on the western diversification department which is being established. Before I get into that though I want to point out to the Member for Kootenay West (Mr. Brisco), who has just spoken, that he should look at the history of the National Energy Program.
If he looks back in Hansard he might find that his Party, in opposition, voted for the National Energy Program and that the New Democratic Party, also in opposition, voted against the National Energy Program. I suggest that before he commits himself in this House and in public he should look back in Hansard and find out who voted for and who voted against the National Energy Program. That does not mean that we did not support some parts of it, as did the Conservatives. I suggest that the Member, who is leaving the House, does not know what he is talking about when he says that the New Democratic Party supported the National Energy Program at its conception.
The Member also made a lot of noise about us voting against a number of programs. He indicates a certain ignorance of what has gone on in this House. We voted against $650,000 for the Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens). If the Government had gone along with us and taken that amount out of the Estimates, we would have supported them. It was quite possible for the Government to do that without affecting any of the other programs which we all supported. The Member should look before he talks. He should not make statements such as he has which are far from accurate.
We voted against $650,000 for that Member but we did not vote against those other things. It was quite possible for the Government to put those Estimates back on the table after removing the amounts about which he spoke.
We in the West have had a lot of experience with diversification and development. The Government changes the name but the hope and the effective help remains about the same, very small. We call the West next-year country and it is this kind of program which makes it next-year country because we have been getting this from Liberal and Conservative Governments for many years. Each time it has come to naught and that is why we are called next-year country, as well as the fact, of course, that we are always looking toward next year's crop. These are the kinds of programs which make us believe that we are indeed next-year country.
The previous Liberal Government launched the Western Development Fund in 1980. It was to be $4 billion over four years, $1 billion a year. It was to start immediately but the money never appeared. It never appeared in the Estimates or as cash on anyone's table in any way. It was diverted. Many of the projects which the Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) indicated the Liberal Government had put before the House and the country already existed. The money was already in the Estimates and had been tagged for these projects but suddenly it became money for the Western Development Fund.
My home city of Prince Albert was in receipt of some of these funds through a program to develop the airport terminal. That terminal had been on the books of the Department of Transport for many years. Suddenly the money became available and was designated as funds from the Western Development Fund even though they were in the Estimates of Transport. We are used to such smoke and mirrors in the West as far as development is concerned. The Liberal and the Conservative versions are not very much different.
We do not really expect too much in the West. We support the idea and the objectives but are very reticent to say that this will happen because too often in the past it has not happened. In this particular case we are told that it is going to be $1.2 billion over each of four years compared with the Liberals' $4 billion over four years. There is quite a difference in the amount, which I do not think makes much difference in determining whether the Liberals had a better program because we never got any money from them either.
What is the source of the funds? According to the Minister, the office of the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion will be closed and its budget and personnel will go to the department of western economic diversification, at a cost of some $11 million. The legislation indicates that the personnel will come from the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, with total operating costs of some $19 million, according to the 1988-89 Estimates.
The $290 million of the $1.2 billion this year for all four provinces is not really new money. In 1985, economic and regional development funds amounted to $14,844 billion, which was reduced each year, to $11,792 billion by 1987, a drop of some $3 billion. Of that $3 billion, $1.2 billion is being restored to the West, some $200 million in the East and further funds for northern Ontario. Therefore, these funds do not necessarily represent new money, and do not even equal the $3 billion that was cut during those three years.
In 1987, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion was operating across Canada with funds of $11,792 billion. That department has disappeared, to be replaced by the department of western economic diversification, the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, FEDNOR for northern Ontario development as well as the Department of Science and Technology. The smoke and mirrors approach taken by the Government means that we are not sure how that $11 billion has been allocated.
It has been suggested that this is not new money in light of the fact that several programs will expire. These include IRDP which will expire this year and the IRDA program which will run out the year after. The Western Transport Industrial Development Fund will terminate after another year. Therefore, the federal Government will no longer have to fund these programs. Furthermore, the personnel for the department will
March 14, 1988

come from the offices of DRIE and Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
The Minister responsible for western economic diversification will be the czar of development in western Canada. When one considers this legislation and the material which has been sent to us, it appears that the department of western economic diversification, although small, will be responsible for the coordination of the line departments, including such major departments as Agriculture and Transport.
The present definition of "Minister" reads:
'Minister' means such member of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada as is designated by the Governor in Council as the Minister for the purposes of this Act'.
The definition in this legislation states:
'Minister', in relation to any class of matters to which this Act extends in any province or region of a province, means such member of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada as is designated by the Governor in Council as the Minister for the purposes of this Act in relation to that class of matters in that province or region of a province;'
It means that this small department will become responsible for the co-ordination of line departments. Hon. Members will know that the Department of Transport is a major department in the West and has a lot of clout. It is very difficult to reverse a decision of the Department of Transport, but that is the responsibility of this department of western economic diversification.
While the concept of having such a department responsible for line departments is good, I doubt that the czar of Western Economic Diversification will have enough power. The Department of Regional Industrial Expansion had the responsibility of co-ordinating line departments in regional development and got nowhere. We know, from experience in the West, that it is a very difficult task.
There is also a danger that the Minister can turn this $1.2 billion into a slush fund to be used as a weapon against governments such as the Manitoba Government or individuals and organizations that do not follow government direction.
I do not believe the Minister will be able to fulfil his responsibility with $60 million a year for each province. The trade deal will not allow him to do the many things the Minister says he wants to do in the booklet he passed out to the House last August. He suggests there are a number of things the trade deal will limit. One of the things the Alberta Government, the Saskatchewan Government, the Manitoba Government, and probably the Ontario Government, have done in the development of small industries and companies in Canada, is to give them breaks with respect to the cost of energy and other resources. That is no longer possible under the trade deal. Under the trade deal we cannot give someone in Canada a break, unless that break is given to his opposition in the United States as well.
Western Economic Diversification Act
A lot of the strength of Canadian development in the West has been in transportation. There are really two ways in which one can support regional development in the West. First is by helping out in the development of the industry or whatever one intends to develop in the West and, second, by developing the kind of transportation structure which makes it possible for western products to reach the market at a price that is competitive with other products from the United States or eastern Canada. We will no longer be able to subsidize transportation. The trade deal limits that. It limits it immediately on things like granola. We think that is one of the directions in which the trade program is going. It does not say so specifically in all areas but it indicates that that is what we can expect.
We cannot give tax breaks. We will be required to input substitution of Canadian products. There is a section in the trade deal which suggests that if the company is working in Canada, it must be treated as if it was local. Therefore, we cannot say that we have a product in Canada which will be used to manufacture something else in Canada more cheaply. The American company can come in and use that product. All of these things are in the trade deal.
Also the idea that we can establish a "buy Canada" or "buy provincial" is going to be left out as well. We might be able to keep our "buy provincial" policies because we do not really have too good a trade between provinces, but we will not again after this trade deal comes into effect be able to have a "buy Canada" policy because it suggests that any product coming into Canada must be treated as if it were produced in Canada.
We are told that 12,000 tonnes of grapes that are produced in British Columbia, the whole wine industry, will be wiped out because we will not be able to protect that industry from its competition in the United States. One of the things the Government has suggested it was going to do, and do well, is to allow supply and services to be divided among all the provinces of Canada. The West is 26 per cent of the population and has only 11 per cent of the procurement of the Government of Canada. The CF-18s, the rail line rehabilitation, the municipal infrastructure, even the so-called diversification fund, are so far all committed to Canada. These have now been committed to Eastern Goodrich and Japanese firms, not to firms which could and do give us a lot of jobs.
I have been critical of the Bill and what is going to happen because of the Bill, but I am not critical of the idea. What we need is development and diversification in the West. We have strong industries in the West. We have agriculture, mining, energy, forestry. These are industries which are very strong and on those industries can be built the kind of economic development which will make the West a prosperous area. I agree that we need this kind of development. I use the words "development" instead of "diversification" because diversification implies something different. But we have the strong industries from which we can develop other industries which

March 14, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
would be important and would make us a strong and viable operation in the West. I have much more to say but the time does not allow.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to participate in support of Bill C-113, which establishes the western economic diversification department. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announced the details of the western diversification initiative last August, he stressed the Government's belief that Canada's regions must have a more direct role in shaping the programs that affect them. In other words, sharing the major decision-making process with the regions.
This initiative builds on ongoing Government action to implement the 1984 Prince Albert Declaration which sets out the fundamental principles that should underlie western Canadian economic development policies, recognition of the importance of providing opportunities to allow young people to remain in the West, the importance of strong western representation in the Cabinet and the need for co-operation, consultation and understanding between the federal Government and the West.
Indeed, we must build on our strengths by providing technical, financial and market opening support to those westerners with a will to win. I might add that, in my view, such a will does exist in the West.
It is important to emphasize that the western diversification fund is not a substitute for spending programs operated by other departments, particularly those active in key resource and economic infrastructure sectors like agriculture, energy, fisheries and transport.
Western diversification investments are seeking to take best advantage of new national policies with respect to such matters as international trade and industrial innovation. This is just one more of our Government's initiatives to add to the overhaul of Canada's finances, the Meech Lake Accord and the free trade initiative.
We have moved on the economic front, the social front, in external affairs and in improving federal-provincial relations, not to mention the 1.2 million jobs created since September 1984 and the fact that there are .5 million fewer Canadians living below the poverty line today than there were in 1984.
The western diversification initiative is further proof that our Government has been sensitive to western needs from the first months we came into office. In my own Province of Alberta, 53,000 jobs have been created since the election and the unemployment rate has fallen from a record of 12.1 per cent in September 1984 to 9.5 per cent. In Calgary it has gone from 13.1 per cent to 8.5 per cent, with 16,000 jobs having been created in the past 12 months. Housing starts are up in Alberta. The value of building permits has increased. Retail sales have increased by 8 per cent in the past year. International tourism has improved in the past year without even taking
into account the influx of tourists brought about by Calgary's magnificent Winter Olympic Games.
In rig activity, there were 328 rigs drilling in February this year compared to 141 at the same time last year. I am proud to say also that the Party which abolished the National Energy Program has come through with special payments to farmers to help overcome the subsidized competition from Common Market countries. With western diversification we are intent on backing up and diversifying the resource sectors of the western economy, but we can also move into developing manufacturing and high-technology fields.
When Prime Minister Trudeau made one of his trips to the West in 1973 Calgary hosted the Western Economic Opportunities Conference that resulted in piles and piles of learned papers. Finally, in the 1980 Budget of his Government the creation of a $4 billion western development fund was announced. To questions I placed on the Order Paper I learned that $345 million of this was assigned to native economic development; $82 million was assigned to an agri-food development program; and $60 million was assigned to a Vancouver rapid transit system. Amounts assigned to western grain transportation related initiatives included $1.7 million, plus increased future commitments under the Western Grain Transportation Act.
However, it was interesting to me to learn that the initiatives associated with the fund were to be financed out of general budgetary revenues, and that the funding was established partly in recognition of the increased revenues anticipated under that devastating Liberal National Energy Program, devastating to the West. In other words, the West was being bled for some narrow initiatives which would do nothing, nothing to diversify its economy, and left it largely dependent on its non-renewable natural resources.
The Western Diversification Program is an entirely new concept. It is one which will co-ordinate all federal economic development activities in the West. The establishment of the headquarters in Edmonton will mean that a significant part of the decision-making on development projects will be shifted west, increasing the understanding of the economic atmosphere in which we must function and eliminating the delays of a distant bureaucracy.
It is planned that the WDO's head office in Edmonton, together with its sub-offices in Vancouver, Saskatoon, and Winnipeg, will use its allocation to top up projects, contribute to important infrastructure projects and aid in the exploration of new ways to expand the potential of our western resource base. Western diversification staff will also assist businesses to find their way through the Ottawa bureaucracy, no mean task. It will help people in the front lines of Canadian economic development. Through these contacts it is hoped, in cooperation with the provinces and the business community, that
March 14, 1988

strengths and weaknesses of local economies can be analysed sector by sector.
This program has been designed to serve as an active and aggressive voice which will ensure that national decisionmaking reflects western opportunities and western needs. Our Government has undertaken to continue to provide the environment in which business can flourish. For instance, new rules for financial institutions are encouraging vigour and competitiveness throughout the financial sector. Tax reform will reduce distortions, promote equity and reward productive investment. The new National Transportation Act will improve Canada's lifelines by removing freight rate discrimination.
With 10 western Members of Cabinet the structure is in place to support them and their policy initiatives. Western Canadians are knowledgeable and aware of how crucial a secured access to the lucrative United States' market is. My constituents have been solidly behind our free trade agreement with that country. At the same time westerners are conscious of the opportunities available in the Pacific Rim. I have noted with satisfaction their pursuit of those markets.
Our Government has shown that it has confidence in Canadians. Entrepreneurs in this country want access to markets and an opportunity to compete because we have the talent to compete with anyone in the world.
I believe the WDO's most significant contribution in the long run will be the strong influence it can bring to bear on behalf of western Canada in the formulation of federal economic development to prepare for the next decade and, indeed, the next century. My personal hope is that WDO will seek high returns in economic development and diversification, monitor the performance of its investments and cut its losses if expectations are not met.
The federal Government has increased dramatically its assistance to the energy and grain producers. This fund is in addition to those substantial amounts.
The energy sector is a vital component of the western economy. Western Canada accounts for approximately 99 per cent of Canada's crude oil and natural gas production. Alberta alone accounts for some 87 per cent of production. Western Canada remains highly dependent on the oil and gas sector as the engine of growth. It is my hope that through programs such as western diversification a broader economic base can be achieved.
When the price of oil declined in early 1986 the economy in the West, and in particular in Alberta and the City of Calgary, declined significantly in terms of jobs lost and serious reduction in investment and exploration activity. Spot prices fell to under $13 U.S. a barrel. In fact, they fell from almost $30 down to below $10 a barrel. With these rapid and unforeseen developments in the oil and gas markets the Governments of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Canada have taken measures to assist the industry and maintain employment.
Western Economic Diversification Act
Alberta announced royalty relief in support programs. Saskatchewan introduced three programs to promote industry activity or reduce royalty burdens. Among the federal Government's provision of tax relief measures and assistance were the elimination of the petroleum and gas revenue tax, the elimination of which the Opposition did not support, and the introduction of the Canadian Exploration and Development Incentive Program which, although it is to be phased out, has supported the industry through these very trying times.
At the federal-provincial-territorial conference of Ministers of Energy in January, 1987, the Ministers agreed to undertake a review of energy security which would include an assessment of the role of conservation, oil substitution, oil and gas transportation infrastructure, electricity and the means to accelerate the development of new energy projects.
The Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources, of which I have the honour to be Chairman, undertook to do a study which we called "Oil: Scarcity or Security?" In particular, our committee's concern was the future availability of crude oil internationally and domestically and the future supply of conventional light crude oil.
Our report clearly indicated the potential for serious problems arising from the highly uneven distribution of the world's light petroleum resources. The committee recognizes that the federal Government must weigh other concerns as well in setting energy policy. The question of oil availability cannot be settled as a resource issue alone. The committee paid due attention to the need for the satisfactory resolution of environmental and native concerns. As Members will know, our committee is not empowered under Standing Orders to undertake studies in environmental or aboriginal issues. However, the committee did feel that it had a responsibility to indicate the implications of making policy which ignores the petroleum supply question.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse), in the Government response to the report, did state that the Government is in general agreement with our observations that Canadian policy should be an intermediate one between the extremes of a laissez-faire approach and the massive intervention typified by the National Energy Program of the previous Government. The Minister went on to state that although the report suggested that strategic intervention should be directed at oil, because oil markets do not function in a normal economic fashion, the Government's approach has been to improve the functioning of domestic energy markets and internationally to co-operate with our trading partners in initiatives designed to improve the stability of international oil markets.
The initiatives already taken by the Government in the energy sector to date will help prevent a loss of technological leadership. Our oil and gas sector is among the most advanced anywhere, and it has benefited from exporting its technological

March 14, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
expertise around the world. Substantial potential for the future growth exists in technology intensive areas within the energy sector, such as oilsands mining and heavy oil recovery and upgrading. While the current unstable world oil price situation may have reduced the immediate urgency to develop alternative energy techniques, energy research and development continue to be extremely essential.
A major contribution to the ongoing diversification of Alberta's economy was announced on December 22 last year. This was a joint federal-provincial financial commitment for the development and construction of an $18 million engineering research facility to the Centre for Frontier Engineering Research called CFER. The federal Government, under the WDO, is providing a $7.75 million capital contribution, with $1 million of this to be matched by CFER through its industry supporters. The Alberta Government is providing a total of $6.75 million, which includes a $4.5 million capital grant, $1.25 million toward operating funds through 1993, and $1 million maximum interest subsidy. The province will also provide a loan guarantee of up to $5 million.
The planned facility will feature two unique world class laboratories, a low temperature structural laboratory and a tubular products laboratory. Research undertaken in the new facility will be aimed at the development of technology to lower both the capital and operating costs of Canada's industry resources.
CFER was established in 1983 with funding from the Devonian Group of Charitable Foundations, the Government of Alberta, and the private sector. It is a non-profit research organization located in Edmonton. Industry support for the research centre has come from some 40 firms, including oil, steel, and engineering consulting companies across Canada.
It is fundamentally important that Canada maintain this technological edge and that the federal Government's actions continue to support the oil and gas sector and help us maintain this advantage. I trust that the WDO will be interested in projects consistent with Canada's international trade policy, which would help firms in the sector to broaden a commercially competitive capacity to apply their considerable expertise to other domestic sectors and to exports.
Support of propane and natural gas fuels development will, I am sure, continue. In the future, non-conventional sources of supply, such as oilsands, heavy oil, plus frontier supplies will become an increasingly large factor in Canada's energy equation. A number of major projects to develop these resources at present being evaluated or under way will have the potential to bring on stream large new oil supplies while increasing Canada's technological leadership.
The importance of Canadian energy security should be coupled with the value and benefit of Canada's energy exports. The goal of security of supply can best be achieved in an
environment that encourages a free international flow of energy commodities.
Since announcing its intention to place a priority on western diversification in the October 1986 Throne Speech, our Government has held numerous informal meetings and discussions with provincial Governments concerning the federal initiative and has welcomed specific proposals from those provinces. The Premiers have established a western ministerial working group on diversification to design, with the Government of Canada, the imminent federal strategy. The federal Government has agreed, with the emphasis placed by the Premiers on the importance of long-term policies, to secure economic stability, growth, and diversification in western Canada.
In conclusion, in preparing the western diversification initiative, the federal Government has listened closely to the advice of western Canadians. A consensus has emerged on the objectives, and the implementation of the western economic diversification department is a major step towards realizing those objectives.
I wish to state my firm support for Bill C-113.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext:
It was an excellent speech given by the Hon. Member for Calgary South (Mrs. Sparrow) which answered many of the questions raised here today about the value and worth of this western diversification program. I would like the Hon. Member to comment on a comment made by the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) when he stated that there would be limitations because of the trade initiative between Canada and the United States.
Of the 262 odd offers for projects that WDO has made in the last five or six months, does the Hon. Member believe that most of those projects that are forthcoming in western Canada are not coming forward because of anticipated exports into that huge market into the United States? Many small businesses and new opportunities in the West seem to be very excited about the opportunities, not of a market of 2 million people or 25 million in Canada, but of the opportunity of moving south of the Alberta and Saskatchewan borders into states that have populations as great as all of Canada. The opportunity now is there because of the openness of the border and the loss of tariff inhibitions that have been there in the past. Even in the energy field workers can cross the border much more freely than they could in the past.
I would like the Hon. Member to comment on whether she believes that a lot of the help that the federal Government can give to western firms will in fact result from the anticipation of a better trading arrangement with the United States?

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext:
I wish to thank my colleague, the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger), for his kind remarks and his questions. To start off I believe that there have already been 4,000 or 4,100 requests for assistance through the western diversification office.
March 14, 1988

The Hon. Member has suggested that 262 projects are being reviewed. Certainly this shows what western Canada has and that we are willing to work toward improving our areas in terms of natural resources and in the agricultural field.
However, in the area of free trade we are looking to a market of not only 25 million people, but of 250 million plus 25 million. We know that in the area of oil and gas it takes moneys invested in certain areas to bring on megaprojects. They are extremely expensive. Also, through high technology, we are working toward becoming more efficient in the production of the tar sands as well as the frontier areas.
In my previous remarks I mentioned CFER which will be built in Edmonton. It will do cold weather research with regard to tubular goods and will allow us to become far more efficient and productive.
I must say that the petrochemical industry is probably the main thrust under free trade. My hon. colleague is absolutely right that free trade will remove some of the tariffs, which go up as high as 18 per cent on some petrochemical products. They have really been a tremendous barrier to allowing us to improve export and production in that particular area.
First, certainly the petrochemical area will benefit a great deal. The second area must be investment. As we improve our efficiency and our ability to do enhanced oil recovery and improve pipeline transportation, I foresee that it will take a lot of investment. This is why I want to say that the Hon. Member is absolutely right. Free trade will allow western Canada to expand and will give us markets so that perhaps we will not be so reliant on a federal Government.
It is very interesting to note that for many years most major decisions have come out of central Canada. It is high time that the regional areas, be they the Atlantic provinces, the western provinces, or northern Ontario, had people with the expertise in their own areas to look at and approve the most beneficial projects in the areas with which they are concerned.
As far as regional assistance under free trade is concerned, of course it has been exempted and will be reviewed. There is nothing in the free trade agreement that will discourage the western diversification office that we are setting up or the $1.2 billion fund. This was clearly set out in the free trade agreement. Canada has so many regions which vary in population and in economics that it is only prudent to realize this and have it included in the free trade agreement.
I look forward to the future of this particular initiative which we have established out West, and I look forward to working with the Minister.

Madam Speaker, when the debate has to do with the West it has a special attraction to me. I would have been sorry to see no one from Quebec say at least a few words. However I do deplore the lateness of the hour-I
Western Economic Diversification Act
always like the thruth-because I have to meet an important group at 7.45 p.m., and I would have liked to speak longer in the debate, but what matters is not how long one speaks, but the feelings one tries to convey as is now the case on this Bill called the Western Economic Diversification Act.

It is well known to all my colleagues that I have a lot of affinity with western Canada. I must have been to western Canada over 200 times, at least to speak, since becoming a Member of Parliament. If there is someone who should understand, it is certainly me. I am from Quebec but I am a federal Member in Ottawa, a Canadian, who understands the importance of western Canada to all Canada.
I just returned from three days in Winnipeg where I saw a very enthusiastic lady, as enthusiastic as the one who spoke before me, Mrs. Carstairs, the leader of the Liberal Party. As the House knows, she will be celebrating her birthday on the same day as she will become the Premier of Manitoba.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext: What does this have to do with western diversification?

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ENDORSE THE MOTION OF MR. MULRONEY
speechtext:
The Hon. Member would be surprised. I have discovered that there is no polarization in Manitoba. Polarization was one of the great difficulties. If people all on one side, decide that they do not like it and go to the other side, there is no middle ground. However, I think that Mrs. Carstairs represents the middle ground and that polarization has been totally destroyed. It is a new ball game in Manitoba. I have a great deal of respect and affection for her. I spoke to a school in which Mrs. Carstairs was a teacher many years ago. She reminded me of that fact on the weekend. I did not remember it, but I was very delighted that she remembered the occasion.
I just wanted to say a few words in a non-aggressive way. It is a call to Canadians. I may not agree totally with the Bill, but it will go to committee. It will be reviewed. Every Government has its own approach to diversification.
Any part of my country is very important to me. Anything that can be done to make Canadians at large, not only western Canadians, understand that if a part of Canada is unhappy- and this is always my speech; people will say: "there he goes again"-the rest of Canada should feel unhappy. If western Canada does not feel that it is part of Canada, the rest of Canada should look into it and take the necessary steps to ensure that all parts of Canada are total parts of Canada and totally happy to be parts of Canada.
If I only have the time to say that-and probably that is all I will have time to say if I look at Madam Speaker-at least I have said it as a Quebec Member, un depute du Quebec a Ottawa, to underline the importance of what we are about to study in the parliamentary committee.
I may not be the greatest expert in law, but I should like to call upon Canadians to understand that when a part of Canada

is unhappy, when a part of Canada is feeling frustrated, or when a part of Canada does not feel that it is getting as much from all of Canada, there will be difficulty. If the Bill, amended or otherwise, could help achieve that goal, I think we will have done a great thing for my country. I will thank the Hon. Member now because I have to go.
